speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: HEADQUARTERS' SITE FOR GAGETOWN BRIGADE TRAINING AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the interest that has been taken in the matter, I think the house might be interested in a brief statement on the selection of the town-site of Gagetown. This has reference to a question by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and is in consequence of other representations.
It was announced on November 15, 1952, that following a thorough investigation by a group of six independent engineers and architects, it had been decided to construct the permanent installations of the army divisional training camp at Gagetown, New Brunswick, in the vicinity of the town of
Oromocto, this site being the most practical under the circumstances. A further announcement on December 3,	1952, gave the
eleven conclusions reached by the six independent engineers and architects following their investigation, which formed the basis of their recommendation of the Oromocto site. Their decision was based on such factors as general topography and soil condition, capacity for expansion and development, water supply, supply of electric power, railway facilities, the proximity of airport facilities and the accessibility of both the main training area and local ranges. Following the announcement of that decision, a delegation of citizens from Saint John, New Brunswick, met with the Minister of National Defence and made representation that the matter should be reconsidered. As a consequence, representatives of the citizens of Saint John, the Department of National Defence and the consulting engineers, met last week at Saint John and visited the alternative Westfield site. When the detailed military requirements were related to the ground in the Westfield area it was decided that it would be more satisfactory and more economical to develop the Oromocto site and the decision announced on November 15, 1952, has consequently been affirmed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as there has been distributed to hon. members a white paper on Canada's defence program for 1953-54 which gives very full information about the program for the current fiscal year, it is not my intention to go into the same facts and figures or to endeavour to cover the same ground.
When we consider the defence program of any country we must realize that its purpose is to produce armed forces. It will be judged by the quantity, quality, selection, training, equipment and leadership of the forces, whether they be in the navy, army or air force and whether they be active or reserve. In the last resort the quality of the forces of any country is tried and tested and proved in battle, and during peacetime in exercises and training operations. So that it seems to us that it is important to keep always in the forefront of our minds the fact that while here in parliament we.are dealing with dollars and cents and in the department often we are dealing with plans and programs, contract demands and requisitions, orders and regulations; but the object of it all is the young man with a rifle and his ability to use it as part of a trained, equipped formation. We should, I submit, in appraising and appreciating what has been done in the way of defence, examine the results, and those results can be seen today in far-off Korea or in Germany or in the various training exercises that have taken place in Canada and elsewhere.
For the first time in peacetime our defence forces, navy, army and air force, have achieved a total of over 104,000, and of those there are officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy in three destroyers constantly on duty, on patrol and in action in the Far East. That has been the case ever since July, 1950. In the course of their operations these ships have sailed a total of 720,000 miles. They have engaged in action and in activities on a scale far above anything experienced by similar vessels in the second world war, and they have shown that if you can judge the quality of the Royal Canadian Navy by their performance there is not much wrong with the Royal Canadian Navy.
At the same time officers and men of the 25th infantry brigade have been in action in Korea. While the strength of the brigade, as is well known, is about 6,000, altogether over 20,000 officers and men have fought with the brigade in Korea. We have followed the practice of rotating men who have been
3806	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence in service there for a year and it has been possible to maintain the practice of rotation. In the course of it, and to replace those wounded now totalling some 1,300, or others who have had to leave the field of battle by reason of illness, it has taken a total of about 20,000 officers and men.
The third battalions of the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Princess Patricia's and the "Van Doos" have left for Korea to begin the third term of rotation. When the United Nations began this international police operation no one anticipated that it would go on for three years. As the Hon. Frank Pace, Jr., former United States secretary of the army, declared before a committee of congress just ten days ago, no one anticipated it; and yet day in and day out there have been Canadians on that front showing that they are as good as any force fighting there.
Simultaneously squadron No. 426 of the Royal Canadian Air Force has been carrying on an airlift to the Far East supplemented by Canadian Pacific Air Lines, both flying North Star aircraft produced by Canadair Limited, and the two services working in close harmony have produced a record of over 900 round trips for a total of close to 12 million miles of successful travel without loss or injury, a record unequalled.
At the same time at the other side of the world we have been building up our forces in Europe, and in the army have contributed the 27th Canadian infantry brigade to the forces under the command of the supreme allied commander in Europe. That completes our army commitment to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Our forces have been there since the target date of November, 1951. In accordance with the procedure decided upon, some 1,913 married men have returned on rotation at the end of a year's service. The force has been maintained and is among those forces on the western front trained and equipped so that it could enter battle at an hour's notice. It also has earned a good record for itself and for Canadian arms.
We have sent abroad a wing of three squadrons of Sabre fighters which are now stationed at North Luffenham, England, and form an important, yes, an important part of the defences of the north Atlantic area in England. They were followed by a second wing in a remarkable operation called "Operation Leapfrog" when all the aircraft of the second wing were flown across by their own pilots to take up their station at Grostenquin, France. A third wing is on the way over and is arriving at Zweibrucken in the French zone of Germany. When I visit it for the first time next week I expect to hand it over to the control of SHAPE and complete


three-quarters of our air force commitment on the target date.
A fourth wing is now being formed in Canada with officers and men joining their squadrons and being equipped with Sabre fighters as they come off the lines and are tested. That wing will leave for overseas later this year to complete the formation of our air division of twelve squadrons of Sabre fighters plus a divisional headquarters, plus a repair depot and the other supporting units, which will complete our air commitment to NATO right on the target date.
Simultaneously our navy has been building up its strength and we have supplied to the forces under SACLANT, the supreme allied commander in the Atlantic, North Atlantic Treaty Organization, all the ships we have promised up to date. We expect to comply with our commitment for the current fiscal year of 1953-54; and, subject to a possible exception which I will mention later, we expect to complete our naval commitment to the North Atlantic treaty on the target date.
At one and the same time we have been discharging our obligations as one of the United Nations in an effort to stop aggression in Korea and, as one of the North Atlantic treaty nations, to build up our forces in Europe so that they, with those of our allies, may form a rampart of peace and preserve our security by being sufficiently strong to indicate to the only potential enemy that he cannot win.
That operation has gone on over a period of less than three years. It is important that hon. members should appreciate that fact. The act of aggression which changed the thinking of the western world took place on June 25, 1950, and the plan under which we began to build up our forces in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization was first approved at Washington in October, 1950. In other words, in less than three years Canada, like the other western nations, has built up its strength very substantially indeed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the plan on which we have been proceeding was announced by me in the house on February 5, 1951. On that occasion I announced that we were embarking on a three-year plan which it was then estimated would cost $5 billion. It was a three-year plan because that was the period which had been agreed to by the North Atlantic treaty nations as being suitable for planning purposes; and the object at that time was to build up our forces collectively so that we would arrive at the strengths that were fixed from time to time by June 30, 1954. Since then, of course, there have been delays in all countries-

delays in construction and the production of equipment, delays sometimes due to financial or economic reasons, and delays contributed to considerably by the continuation of hostilities in Korea and in other parts of the world. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization recognizes this situation and uses a new word "slippage" to describe it.
There has been some slippage and, generally speaking, the date now fixed as the target for the achievement of the program as revised from time to time is June 30, 1955. As I say, having completed our army commitment already, having every expectation of completing our air force commitment this year, and having completed our navy commitment up to date and expecting to do so for the next year, we expect to complete our planned program, subject to one or two exceptions which I will mention later, by the date originally indicated-by June 30,
1954.
As we go on, some countries will give consideration to a deliberate stretch-out of their programs in order to keep production lines in operation. Rather than accumulate large stockpiles of equipment such as ships, aircraft, guns and ammunition over and above what appears to be immediately required, and over and above reasonable reserves, participating countries will wish to keep items of that kind in production to maintain production lines and keep up productive capacity, rather than to stockpile and close them down. However, in Canada we have not started to do that. The only deliberate stretch-out that we have had has been in connection with the production of the CF-100 and the F-86E aircraft, both of which we deliberately delayed in order to begin production of later types at the earliest possible dates. Neither of those stretch-outs will affect our ultimate position.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that it would be of some convenience to hon. members if we looked at this three-year program and saw how much of it had been achieved and how much it has cost. We can do that now because two of the three years have passed. We have the actual expenditures for the year 1951-52, we have an estimate of the expenditures for the year 1952-53 which has just been completed, but it is likely to be an accurate estimate as it is on the basis of eleven months' experience and a projection for the rest of the fiscal year. Also, we have before us the estimates which we are now discussing for the year 1953-54. The figures which I will give you are divided under the heads which are customary in 68108-2411
Supply-National Defence NATO and which are used in the table appearing in the white paper at page 37. The heads are: Military personnel costs; procurement of equipment; construction; operations and maintenance.
We have expended or will expend during the period 1951-54 a total of $1,164 million on military personnel. That has been the cost of maintaining-paying, feeding and clothing our forces in the navy, army and air force during that period. The total strengths as at April 1, 1953, on the basis of the last figures available but which are subject to correction, are: 15,546 for the navy; 48,458 for the army; 40,482 for the air force; or a total of 104,486 in the active force, and 5,325 for the navy; 47,318 for the army; and 5,760 for the air force; or a total of 58,403 in the reserve force.
There has been some talk about the cost of a man in the armed forces for a year, so I will give the actual figure for the cost of another rank for his initial year on joining the armed forces. The cost is $2,251 per year based on figures most lately determined, without travel or transportation but covering items of pay and allowances, subsistence, clothing, medical and dental services, and pension. That figure is broken down as follows: Pay and allowances $1,135; subsistence, $732; maintenance of clothing and personal equipment, $136; medical and dental service, $43; government contribution to the pension fund, $205; for the total I mentioned of $2,251. Now, for all other ranks for the same period, giving proper weight to the number of men in each grade and pay group, the average cost is $3,023 per year. If we take the average for all three services, for all officers and men, again weighted so as to give the proper weight to the number of officers, their ranks and so on, with the N.C.O.'s and men, the figure is $3,411. The comparable figure for 1949 was $2,975. The comparable figure for all other ranks in 1949 was $2,573, whereas it is $3,023 today, the difference being largely represented by increases in pay and some increases in the cost of living reflected in the items I have mentioned. A comparable figure for all civil servants in the civil service is $2,526. If we take all the civil servants, exclusive of prevailing rate employees and casual labour, their average salary is $2,526, and that compares with the figure for the armed forces of $3,023. They are not very far apart, having regard to the different functions that they perform.
Now, of the members of the armed forces, 43 per cent are married today. This has led us, of course, to the necessity for establishing campsites with married quarters, chapels,

Supply-National Defence schools, stores and all the other amenities of the average civilian community. For example, today the Department of National Defence operates 40 schools for the children of serving personnel, and in those schools there are close to 10,000 children and about 400 teachers, all working in accordance with and under.the provincial educational systems. In the armed forces today we have, largely in the R.C.A.F., 3,200 women who are included in the figures I mentioned above.
Turning to the category of officers, which is of great importance, we have in training today for the active and reserve forces a total of 7,957 men, of whom 4,612 are at the universities. During this last fiscal year we made two major changes in the provisions for the training of officers. The first was the establishment in September, 1952, of the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean, at Saint-Jean, Quebec. I should like to say a word about that institution, which was started in September, 1952, some three months after it had been decided to establish it there. The response, both from the Frenchspeaking and from English-speaking candidates, was very good indeed. The number originally intended to be taken in in the first year of 100 had to be increased to the maximum capacity we could handle, 125. Of the 125, some 78 were of French-speaking origin and the balance were of Englishspeaking origin. In view of the experience of the last six months it can be said that this college, which was certainly new in military training arrangements in this country and in most others, has already proven itself to be a substantial success. The candidates of the two languages mix and work together, and virtually all of them now speak both languages. These men will constitute an important pool of officers of great value, particularly today when the nations of the world are intermingling more freely.
Another important thing is that of the 123 candidates now in attendance, all except 7, if my memory serves me correctly, have signed on with the regular forces and consequently after they graduate from Saint-Jean, and possibly R.M.C., will enter the regular forces, if they qualify, and serve for three years. More and more, we are looking to the graduates who enter the three services colleges of Saint-Jean, R.M.C. and Royal Roads, to be of a category who will sign on for a minimum of three years' service with the regular forces. The balance will serve with the reserve forces.
This brings me to an announcement I should like to make for the first time today. So great has been the success of Saint-Jean, and so desirable is it that this operation in military training as well as in national unity should

be extended, we are going to make provision for a total strength of 400 cadets.
The second development of major proportions made during the year in the training of officers was the establishment of the regular officers training plan, under which cadets at R.M.C., Royal Roads, Saint-Jean or any one of the university plans, may sign on at any stage of his course and receive tuition, subsistence, clothing and so on, and serve as a subordinate officer taking the summer courses, conditional upon his agreement to serve with the regular forces for three years after graduation. It is too early to say what the results of these various devices will be, but our expectation is that, by one means or another, through the services colleges, through the universities or through direct entry on short-service commission basis, we will be able to meet all the requirements to replace the wastage of officers which it is estimated will be of the magnitude of 1,500 from 1954 on. This applies now for the first time, I am glad to say, to doctors and some other officers requiring professional qualifications. Hon. members may recall that I reported earlier that we were short, and we expected to remain short, of doctors. However, owing to improvements in the arrangements we have made, and also to our having recruited a certain number of doctors in the British Isles, the situation is such now that we believe we will have enough doctors, dentists and most other professional personnel to fill all requirements as they arise,
Turning from the question of personnel to that of equipment, I may say that in 1951-54 we have spent or will have spent a total of $2,102 million on equipment. Main items of equipment include ships, of which we now have some 52 on order, of types varying from the aircraft carrier H.M.C.S. Bonaventure which is being built for us on the other side to replace the Magnificent, or the arctic patrol vessel the Labrador, or the escort vessels and minesweepers down to gate vessels. We expect to be behind in the program with regard to the construction of anti-submarine escort vessels. This is accounted for partly by the fact that these are ships of an entirely new type never before built here or anywhere else. We had delays in procuring steel, component parts and machine tools from other countries. The ships are so complicated that the engineering-particularly the electrical engineering-took more time than we had engineers to do the work. I anticipate that there will be some delay with others of these ships as they come off. I also anticipate that they will still be well ahead of any corresponding vessels being made by any other country because we got started on this operation well in advance of the others.

Another major item of equipment is aircraft. It may be remembered that in 1951, in my statement then, I announced that we would require a total of over 3,000 new aircraft. We expect to have by the end of the current fiscal year over 2,000 of those; and we will complete the balance of the planned figure, which is considerably above 3,000 of new aircraft, early in 1955. We have deliberately postponed the equipping of our own forces with additional Sabre fighters in order to make Sabres available to the United States and to Britain. The delay in finishing our own aircraft program will not delay our ful-fulling our commitments to NATO and will not delay beyond the target dates the buildup of our own air force for the defence of Canada, but it will delay the re-equipment of auxiliary squadrons with CF-lOO's and the provision of reserve aircraft.
With regard to weapons such as guns, we have had a large program under way; and here again we expect, for the reasons I have stated, that we shall not be able to complete the whole by March 31 or June 30, 1954, but we should be able to comply with our commitments. The same thing applies to ammunition. Apart from these items we expect that our production of equipment will meet all our requirements. The figures before hon. members already reflect some reduction, as we have completed the program for the stockpiling of a large part of what are called "soft goods" such as clothing and barrack stores.
The next major head of expenditure is construction. Between 1951 and 1954 we have spent or shall have spent a total of $665 million. Between April 1, 1952, and February 28, 1953-that is in the first eleven months of the fiscal year just completed- orders were placed bringing the total value of contracts under administration to $358,398,000, on 1,048 major construction projects plus a larger number of minor ones. Hon. members may appreciate how large an operation this has been when I tell them that during the year 1940-41 we spent on construction a total of $92 million and, during the wartime peak, a total of $152 million

that was in the year 1943-44-whereas at the present time we are administering contracts for a total of $358 million, more than twice the wartime peak. Included in the construction have been buildings for operations, research laboratories, barrack blocks, cookhouses and all the others but, in addition, some 16,550 permanent married quarters which, with the temporary married quarters that we have, make a total of about 20,000 married quarters. We shall still have to continue the married quarters program. The construction program has passed its peak, and this has resulted this
Supply-National Defence year in a lower appropriation for construction, and we believe this figure will be still further reduced next year.
The fourth major head is operations and maintenance. That means the oil and fuel and the repair work necessary to maintain the forces and to enable them to carry on their operations. For the years 1951 to 1954 the total spent or expected to be spent under these heads is $1,301 million.
To summarize these items of cost for the years 1951-54 as actually spent or estimated: personnel, $1,164 million; equipment, $2,102 million; construction, $665 million; operation and maintenance, $1,302 million: or a total of $5,233 million. In addition the excess of credits to the replacement account over expenditures therefrom within this period of $35 million brings the total to $5,268 million. That is on account of the program, announced on February 5, 1951, of $5 billion. It represents an expenditure of 5 per cent over the estimate; but, as I have indicated, there will be some additional expenditures carried into 1954-55 owing to delays in production to which I have referred.
This total includes the amount of $680 million spent or expected to be spent during the period on mutual aid. In the white paper, at page 33, hon. members will see outlined all the expenditures made up to date on mutual aid. They run back to a year before the 1951 period to which I have just referred, and up to March 31, 1953, they total $551,800,000. In addition, in the estimates put before hon. members, there is provided a total of $324 million.
These figures represent, of course, large sums; and the magnitude of the operation that this has involved for the various government departments concerned can be appreciated by one or two comparisons. A large part of the moneys appropriated for national defence is not spent by the Department of National Defence itself. The spending is administered by the Department of Defence Production, in the procurement of equipment; by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in the provision of married quarters; by Defence Construction Limited, in the provision of other buildings; by the Department of Transport in the acquisition of land and in the construction and lengthening of runways. Altogether, during the fiscal year 1952-53 this operation has involved the placing of a total of 151,000 contracts. We have spent on what might be called capital account-that is, for construction and equipment: $2,102 million on equipment and $665 million on construction- making a total of $2,767 million which we have spent or will have spent between 1951 and 1954.

With regard to the reserves, I could give a number of facts and figures. We started this period with some 47,000 officers and men in the reserves and today there are 58,000 despite the fact that some 11,000 of the most active officers and men have joined the active forces from the reserve forces. The number undergoing summer training and taking courses has steadily increased. However, like other hon. members I feel that this very important part of our defence activities deserves every support we can give it. We are constantly discussing with representatives of the conference of reserve associations ways and means of making the work of the reserve more effective.
During recent weeks developments have occurred in the Far East and elsewhere which must have struck hon. members. The communists have shown a disposition to at least open discussions that may lead to a settlement of hostilities in Korea. We welcome that possibility. The peaceful objectives of the western nations have been shown both at the United Nations in New York and in the resumption of negotiations in Korea.
But we must remember that no change has occurred to alter the policy which the United Nations in Korea and the North Atlantic nations have agreed to, that is to build up sufficient strengths so that they can be secured. President Eisenhower and Mr. Churchill have made plain in their statements what I believe is the attitude of all the western nations on this subject. As the Financial Post said on April 4, 1953:
If, today, all the guns on all the fronts where East is fighting West were to be silenced, our side would still be far from achieving the unity, the economic and armed strength essential to our safety.
The western nations have had as their objective the stopping of aggression in Korea and the preventing of aggression in Europe. They have worked together in both areas in a great demonstration of common purpose and common practice to bring about both objectives. This is the first time in the history of the world that nations have agreed on a plan, on an objective and on the ways to achieve it, and nothing has happened to change that objective or to change that plan. We have spent great sums on our defence in Canada, as have other western nations, sums expended as insurance of peace, and the prudent man does not stop paying the premium if the risk continues. While, therefore, everyone is hopeful that what is taking place in Korea may lead to a termination of hostilities there and may lead to a better atmosphere everywhere else, there is no


reason yet for the North Atlantic treaty nations, or those of the United Nations who think with us, to change fundamentally the policy and the course to which they have agreed and to which they put their hands three years ago.
Our hope is that it may be possible to moderate what we are doing, but to change it fundamentally would be a serious indication of weakness. The fact is that the Russians have shown a change of attitude, and. in our view, and I think in the views of those in the other western nations, something which has contributed to that change has been the attitude shown in Korea and the building up of our strength in Europe and at home. That has been our objective, and the fact that we have had three years without a major war has indicated that the policy has so far been right. That policy has, I believe, had the strong support of all sections of the Canadian people as it has had the strong support of members in every part of the house. It is because of that support, because of that great objective and the appeal of that objective to our own people, that the government has seen fit to ask parliament for the large sums of money which we consider necessary to maintain and build up our strength. It is in that spirit that I put before this committee these estimates.

Now, I will turn to the white paper which was issued to us yesterday and I will also refer to the white paper which initiated this program in February of 1951. In the original white paper, the program of 1951, the objectives of our national defence policy are laid down. The minister at that time referred to them as being clear and simple. They are repeated in the program issued yesterday and I will just take a moment to read them because I think they still remain, and I am certain they still remain, as the objectives for which we are working.
(1)	The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(2)	implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or other agreement for collective security;
(3)	the organization to build up strength in a total war.
In other words, we are to make preparations against the risk of communist policy forcing us to defend ourselves against direct attack while, at the same time, meeting our overseas obligations. To a very considerable extent these objectives overlap, because by building up our forces both at home and abroad they will soon become in a position to be a powerful deterrent against aggression; and they will also be in a better position to fight wherever required should global war be forced upon us.
As I have said, these objectives have not been changed. They have been endorsed from the beginning by the members of this party. In fact, this party has repeatedly urged and encouraged the government to achieve these objectives. The means of achieving them and the rate of progress towards their achievement has given and still continues to give this party considerable concern. When the Korean war broke out, and when it became necessary for this country

The right course had to be found and, having been found, it had to be followed. Mr. Chairman, I should like now to refer to the part the army has been assigned, and the progress it has made toward achieving the objectives outlined in the program of February, 1951. The 25th brigade in Korea and the 27th brigade in Europe have been maintained at the strengths up to which it was decided in February, 1951, to have those formations recruited, and it would be churlish on my part if I did not refer to the efforts made by the minister to live up to the obligations he then accepted. We in this party, on this side of the house, are pleased that the government has been able to maintain our overseas detachments of the army at the strength promised to the United Nations and to the NATO organization.
But that strength has been maintained at some expense to the forces being provided for the direct defence of Canada. The program of 1951 included an airborne striking force, anti-aircraft artillery and other units for the defence of Canada against direct attack. When the Korean operation started it was decided that it would not be expedient to send the regular units of the army which at that time were embodied in the striking or mobile airborne force for the direct defence of Canada, and for that reason second battalions of the three regular regiments and the artillery regiment were recruited as ad hoc formations.
Unfortunately it has not been possible to maintain that policy. The airborne striking force has already been broken up and its personnel distributed not only among the forces raised for Korea but also the forces sent with the 27th brigade, with the result that today we have no striking force of units which have been accustomed to work together and which have carried out any extensive training under arctic conditions.
If we are to have units organized and trained to meet an airborne invasion from the north, then those units should have extensive practice in northern areas and, if possible, should be stationed there. In the pamphlet issued by the minister yesterday, in which this year's program is set out, attention is called to the fact that a substantial increase is to be made in the emphasis placed on


the defence of North America against air attack. Well, I should think so! We from this side of the house have been emphasizing ever since 1947 the importance of providing home defence. I have been called various names. It has been suggested that I was an isolationist and that I was an alarmist; and last year I was accused of being a yes-but man. Well, perhaps it will be recognized now that I was a realist, and that I had pointed out the danger of attack on this country, and the necessity for the government to maintain an effective force which would be prepared to meet any airborne attack which might be delivered against our shores.
The mobility of such a striking force would be governed very largely by its ability to be transported by air. We have no transport squadrons available for that purpose. We are told in the white paper that Bristol freighters and C-119 aircraft are being obtained. Well, they are not here now; and even if they were obtained, their range of manoeuvrability would be very considerably handicapped by the lack of airfields in our northern areas.
The fact also remains that in this mobile striking force no provision is made for engineer units trained in the rapid construction of airfields. At the present time such a force would be entirely tied down to the existing airfields, and I think if it is to be a really mobile tactical force it must have included in its organization engineer units capable of and fully trained in the laying down of new airfields and familiar with airfield construction.
Reference was made to anti-aircraft artillery. In his remarks today the minister said that such batteries as we have for the antiaircraft defence of this country, particularly in the reserve army, are armed with obsolescent weapons. I would go much further than that, and say that they were armed with obsolete weapons quite out of date and incapable of engaging a modern bomber which might be sent here. The old Bofors guns which is the equipment of many of the light ack-ack batteries across this country would be quite useless against a modern aircraft. I doubt very much whether they provide the right type of training for our antiaircraft gunners. In fact there is considerable discouragement among the personnel of the anti-aircraft units by reason of the fact that they have such out-of-date equipment.
In so far as the mobile force is concerned, at the moment they have no aircraft which would be capable of acting as fighters to escort them. Without airfields and without fighter escorts to convoy the transports I feel that our mobile force is in a hopeless condition. It has not trained; it has not carried

out many exercises, if any, at the unit level or any operations which it would be called upon to do in the future. They are confined largely to parachute operations because of a lack of landing fields.

I notice from the white paper that since I spoke in the house a year ago a certain number of Centurion tanks have been issued to a squadron-it is only a squadron-with the 27th brigade. The minister referred to the large number of men who have passed through that formation. The formation has a strength of some
6,000	personnel, I think he said, and something over 20,000 have passed through in rotation or have been brought back as casualties. This rotation policy may be pleasant for the personnel serving in the brigade; it is nice to think that a married man will be in Europe for only a year and that the single personnel will not have to stay away from Canada for more than two years. But the policy is extremely expensive and has the detrimental effect of breaking up the units.
A continual change of personnel is not healthy for the maintenance of morale. This applies particularly to infantry units where it is most desirable that the men serve with their regiments and regard their regiments as being their service homes for as long a period as possible. Where you have certain personnel coming back after twelve months and others rotating at different periods it has a serious effect on the development of esprit de corps.
I know that I am an old soldier and that 25 years or more ago we placed a great deal
Supply-National Defence of emphasis upon regimental spirit. I sometimes wonder whether the army of today emphasizes that aspect to the same extent. It was with considerable interest that I read an article last January in the Canadian Army Journal by Major Garber, who was emphasizing the need for maintaining personnel in their regiments as long as possible while serving in Korea. He points out the dangers of frequent changes of personnel and emphasizes the necessity of ensuring that a larger proportion of what he terms capable men be sent to the infantry. I should like to make two brief quotations from this article, which is entitled "Every Rifleman Must be An Aggressive Fighter". I commend the article to the attention of all those who are interested in the problem of maintaining morale and efficiency in our units.
The first extract which I should like to quote is to be found on page 23 and is as follows:
The allocation to Infantry of men who fail to meet the standards set by another corps is a common and dangerous practice for it contributes to inefficiency in a corps that is vital to Canada's defence.
I feel that attention should be drawn to that. Then later on, referring to something which the hon. member for Broadview had advocated a couple of years ago, he states that the soldiers who actually fight should receive danger pay, and he goes on to say:
Many men in specialized corps are given educations at army expense which enhance their opportunities on return to civilian life, but the skills taught infantrymen In most cases, cannot be applied to civilian occupations. They have nothing to show for their years of service except the knowledge of a job well done. Additional pay for fighting men would help to equalize the rewards of service. It is ridiculous to deny fighting men these small rewards on the basis that the administrative effort required is too great. If the task requires longer hours of work from the staff, it would be a small sacrifice to make in comparison to that of the front-line infantrymen.
I am inclined to think that the feeling of the Canadian infantryman today is very much the same as it was during the first world war, because I would have voiced much the same sentiments a good many years ago.
I should like to refer now to the endeavours which have been made to live up to our commitments in respect to the reserve forces. That is the sorry plight-I repeat, the sorry plight-in which we find our reserve army at the present time. It is reported in the white paper that the reserve army had a strength of 47,300 at the end of February of this year. I cannot help feeling that that strength is padded by a good many thousands because when we look at a return submitted earlier in the session in answer

Supply-National Defence to a question we find that only 13,715 out of the 47,300 attended training in camp last year. That 13,000 odd is made up of some 3,850 officers and 9,865 non-commissioned officers and men. If the strength of the reserve army is indeed 47,300, I feel that we are training but a very small fraction of the strength.
After all is said and done, the effective strength of the reserve army lies in the trained personnel in that force. In the past we have voted large sums of money, both last year and in previous years, and the fact that we only trained some 13,000 men for short periods in the summertime bears out my statement that we are only getting meagre returns for the money which has been expended. In other words, the reserve army needs a thorough reorganization at the present time. It must be modernized and it must be provided with the equipment and the facilities to attract the right type of recruits. You cannot expect men to give up their evenings after finishing work at their ordinary civilian occupations to go and train on obsolete anti-aircraft guns. It may be that some of the inefficient units will have to be eliminated. But this is a source of manpower which we must find a way of building up.
As the minister pointed out, this force has also been handicapped by the fact that it has sacrificed itself in making a contribution of some 11,000 men, I think he said, to the active army during the last year. That is highly creditable so far as the units are concerned and is indicative of the desire of the commanding officers who have released these men to take the broadest possible view of conditions. It points out the value of our reserve forces. All through the years our reserve army has provided the means for the expansions that have been necessary when war has broken out. We should be very careful in seeing that our reserves from this source are not weakened, and additional encouragement is required in order to make them effective at the present time. So much for the army.
I have a few remarks I should like to make with respect to the Royal Canadian Air Force and the part that it is playing and should play in the fulfilment of the objectives which were outlined. In the first place I think we must call attention to the dangerous weaknesses which existed in our air force when the Korean conflict commenced. Again it is only fair to give credit to the last-minute efforts that have been made by the government to build up our air forces. But if credit is due to the government for building


up our air forces at the eleventh hour, then blame must also be attached to the government for having allowed those forces to sink to such a dangerous level prior to the outbreak of the Korean disturbance.
In the last few years the air force has received a great proportion of the defence vote. It is receiving now as much in the way of money as is being spent on the other two services. Yet the progress which is being made in the R.C.A.F. still causes us considerable concern. The program of 1951 called for 40 regular and reserve squadrons with more than 3,000 aircraft in addition to aircraft which were in existence in 1951 and of types, so the program indicated, suitable for the purposes for which they were intended. We have been told today, now that more than two-thirds of the three-year period has elapsed, that we have some 2,000 aircraft out of the 3,000, but it is highly questionable whether they are of types suitable for the work for which they were intended. So far as the twelve squadrons of jet fighters for the air division in France are concerned, I believe nine of them are now in Europe and the other three are just in the process of organization. Thus we have very little fighter strength in this country. I understand there are some nine auxiliary fighter squadrons-distributed throughout the length and breadth of Canada from Montreal to Vancouver-which are equipped with world war II Mustangs and more or less worn-out British-built Vampires.
Our fighters have all been sent out of the country with the exception of one squadron of CF-lOO's at North Bay which is today only in the process of being organized. Therefore we have nothing at the moment with the exception of the one squadron of CF-lOO's now being organized, three squadrons of Sabre jets now earmarked for NATO and preparing to move to Europe, and the nine squadrons of the auxiliary air force armed with very indifferent equipment quite incapable of meeting any hostile bombers which might possibly be sent to attack us here. Even the CF-100 squadron at North Bay is far from operational yet. There are difficulties with respect to organization and the supply of ground personnel, and so far as equipment is concerned there are difficulties with respect to the machines and the engines which still have to be ironed out.
In fact the minister in his white paper said that the aircraft we are now producing will eventually become obsolete. I suppose all aircraft will eventually become obsolete, but time is moving very fast. In fact, I do not think I am exaggerating in the least if

I say that in effect Canada has no air defence to direct attack at present, nor is she likely to have for many months to come. Our fighters are non-existent. If we are to rely upon these auxiliary fighter squadrons to produce the direct defence of Canada, it must be realized that they will very soon have to be equipped with aircraft not less efficient than the CF-100; and it takes a very long time to train pilots and to organize ground crews when the personnel of the fighter squadrons are working solely on a part-time basis. No matter how interested the individuals concerned may be, no matter how much time they are prepared to devote to the study of their work, I am very doubtful whether the auxiliary squadrons can be brought up to that state of efficiency which will enable them to be considered as first-line defence against air attack here in Canada. They will require a larger infusion of regular personnel than they have at present. I am not at all sure that we should not place the squadrons to be equipped with CF-lOO's on a regular basis.
Air commitments to NATO have been met but our air arm at the moment is insufficient to meet our NATO commitments without stripping, as has been done, units in Canada which are for the defence of Canada. We are told that we should defend Canada as far away from Canada as possible. That is a delightful dream, but in order to be effective, arrangements would have to be made with the enemy that they would attack Canada as far away from Canada as possible.
Hear, hear.

We might possibly send all our troops down to the Falkland islands, and they could not get very much farther away, but I question whether we would be doing very much for the defence of Canada if we did that. The long and the short of this matter seems to me to be that we have left our front door wide open while we have sallied out through the back door.
The government has spent millions in developing a specific plane, the CF-100, for our own defence; but until that plane is produced in sufficient numbers, and until ground crews are trained, Canada remains without adequate defence at home-and as far as I can see that condition is going to last for many months yet to come. We are told now that:
In the event of an all-out war the most probable method of attack on the North American continent would be by air.
It goes on:
The possibility of such an attack will increase as further progress is made in the design and produc-
Supply-National Defence tion of new aircraft and the increasing stockpile of atomic weapons estimated to be held by the U.S.S.R.
Obviously now the admission is made that the communists could, if they wished, use their stockpile of atomic bombs and use their modern bombers, bombers which are capable of flying 6,000 miles or more if they adopt methods of refuelling in the air, against Canada; and we have nothing here in Canada at the present time to meet such an attack.
No wonder the minister says that the emphasis must now be changed in order to meet such a direct attack on Canada. I fear that until we have built up our defences for this country many Canadians are going to sleep very uneasily in their beds in the months to come. If the international situation, which for the moment seems to have cleared a little bit, should deteriorate again, then I fear that we shall sleep uneasily in our beds until we are provided with the necessary fighter squadrons to beat off any enemy bomber attack which might be directed against our cities. This is nothing new. I have spoken about this matter in the house time and time again. I think it was only last year that I used these words:
The need of maintaining adequate fighter squadrons in Canada for the protection of our industrial plants, the loss of which would create such a crippling blow to our NATO effort and might prove fatal to Canada . . . must not be lost sight of.
I am afraid that it was lost sight of but I am delighted to see that recognition is now being given to the fact that Russian bombers, their TU-4's which have been tried out, are capable of coming here; and steps must be taken to defend Canada against the possibility of such an attack. It is no good to merely refer to our radar screen-if a radar screen exists-because, if it is sufficiently far away from the immediate targets to which it is going to give warning, it must be remembered that it can only be a warning system. There is no defence in radar. Radar can merely give a warning of the approaching enemy; and, unless the radar stations are in the extreme northland, it can only be a warning of a matter of four or five hours at most before a modern bomber could reach our industrial cities.
If you have no defence-and we have no anti-aircraft defence and we have no fighters -then all you can do is to tell people to run and hide. That is all the defence that radar can give you. It is no wonder that a man like Wing Commander Rohmer should have felt that it was his duty to speak in the city of Toronto just a few weeks ago and to say that Canada is absolutely defenceless to air

Supply-National Defence attack at the present time in spite of the millions which have already been spent on air defence.
I could go on a great deal longer on the question of air but I do not feel that I am entitled to detain the committee much longer. However, I just want to refer to the question of construction which has been going on.
The minister referred to the fantastic sums which have been spent on construction in this country, but there is other construction going on in Europe and foreign countries. The amount spent between April 1, 1950, and December 31, 1952, is, I think, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $358 million for projects in Canada, exclusive of married quarters. That construction can be divided into accommodation such as barracks and so forth, into amenities such as canteens, recreation rooms, swimming pools, schools, hospitals and so forth; and technical buildings such as workshops, administrative buildings and hangars. I would like the minister to explain the policy which is being followed in connection with this big construction program.
Some of these buildings which are being constructed are of a permanent nature, others semi-permanent and still others are purely temporary. We understand the purposes to which the temporary buildings will be put; they are to meet the immediate situation. But what plan is being followed, if any, in respect to the erection of permanent and semi-permanent buildings? Where are those being placed, and for what number of troops to be permanently employed in Canada are those buildings designed? Elsewhere, the methods of construction and the methods of awarding the contracts have been examined. We are not satisfied with all of this construction work, some of which I have seen. In a great many cases, the contracts are being let without calling for tenders. The contracts are being let on a cost-plus basis, and they are an invitation to extravagance. There is the feeling that such extravagance has taken place. Everyone wishes to have our troops comfortably housed and our servicemen provided with all the amenities, but nothing is to be gained by such expenditures as those which have been disclosed in the press and elsewhere.
Now, to sum up my rather lengthy remarks, I feel that the program which was drawn up in 1951, which is still being adhered to, and the progress which has been made shows that, although two-thirds of the time for this three-year program has elapsed, the objectives are not really in sight. Secondly, already the

estimated $5 billion has been found inadequate and is being exceeded. Thirdly, much of the huge sum of money that has been spent has been spent on non-essentials, with the result that the taxpayer has not received full value in terms of defence for the outlay of his dollars. Fourthly, Canada today is virtually defenceless against air attack, although such attack is now admitted as a possibility. Fifthly, no mobile tactical force, combining the army and R.C.A.F. units, for defence against airborne attack on Canada exists. Sixthly, the reserve army, because of lack of training facilities, is ineffective and requires complete reorganization before it can play its role in the defence of Canada in total war. Lastly, our naval construction program lags far behind schedule.
It is for these reasons that we have criticized the progress that has been made in the development of this program which was laid down in 1951.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure you will agree with me that any backbencher entering this debate does so with a lot of diffidence. Most of the members of this house are not able to obtain the kind of information necessary to enable them to discuss the defence program. In my opinion national defence is a misnomer. What we are engaged in is a global defence. Canada is merely one part of a team that has been organized through the United Nations to provide an international police force to police the peace of the world. If we are going to do that job successfully it is going to cost money. We are going to have to pull our share of the load, and merely carping criticism based on a lot of misinformation is not going to serve any useful purpose. The opinions which I shall express are based on the information it is possible for an ordinary member of the house to obtain.
We are going to have to ask ourselves some questions, and answer them honestly, in order that the people who pay the taxes to provide this program may have some understanding of the necessity for the continuation of the program upon which we have embarked. The first question we have to ask ourselves is whether or not peace is any closer today than it was when we first made the appropriation of $5 billion and allocated it for the purpose of defence. In my opinion, it is not. I have seen a lot of comment in the press, and I have heard a lot of opinions expressed to the effect that the new tactics employed by Russia are an indication that that nation is ready to put out the hand of peace and do away with the armaments race. It is said that, therefore, our defence effort is no longer necessary.

In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the new Russian approach to the international problem is not a change of policy at all, but merely a change of tactics. I know that many members of this house have read a lot of the philosophy and the program of communism as laid down by Marx, brought up to date by Lenin and Stalin, and now Malenkov has the job of carrying that program forward and bringing it up to date. I say it is merely a change of tactics because in the past I have had tc contend with a lot of these people. You have to read about their philosophy and policies if you are going to successfully talk to them in the many places that you meet them. Since 1945, and up until recently, we have been going through part of a program, as far as communism is concerned, that was laid down a good many years ago. Since 1945 we were in the period which they termed the national revolutions, in which they would stay at home to build up their own country, promote revolution in every other country, just as they have right across Europe and Asia, and then let the revolution take place on the inside of that country. That period is over.
The communists tell you quite frankly in their literature that in the struggle for world revolution there will be periods of attack, retrenchment and retreat. They are merely in a period of retrenchment to consolidate the gains which they have made, then they will go forward when the opportune time arrives. In my opinion, the program upon which we have embarked for global defence to build an international police force to police the peace of the world is just as necessary now as it was when we made that appropriation. I think that has to be made clear to our people. We have to make it clear that we are living in a world in which there are no frontiers, no barriers; it is one world. Our defences are going to have to be kept up, I believe, during the lifetime of most members of this house.
I have listened to a lot of criticism in the house, and I have read a lot in the press, concerning waste and extravagance. I could stand up here perhaps and make that kind of criticism myself. But I should just like to say this. When we made the appropriation of $5 billion and said that we were going to build an army, a navy and an air force and everything that is necessary to supplement those organizations, we were in the position where we went out into the country and took in civilians from all over Canada, people who were untrained, gave them a few months o' military training, made officers of them, put stars on their shoulders and then sent them in to head up a department that was going
Supply-National Defence to spend perhaps a billion dollars. The spending of money and the keeping of books requires a great deal of training and in the process of throwing that money around there was bound to be a good deal of waste, not because of dishonesty but, in my opinion, because of inefficiency. In many of the documents that I have seen, and with the eight or nine accounting systems that existed, for example, in the works branch of the army, I think there was a clear indication that there were on jobs a great many people who should not have been on them, and as a result there was created the mess that necessitated the Currie report.
I say that the minister himself and his department are responsible for permitting that kind of thing to develop. As the minister will recall, for two years, as one member of this group-and there were others in the house-I suggested that the minister should take under consideration the appointment of an additional minister. I pointed out that it was not humanly possible for one minister to preside over the three defence departments, with the reorganization that was bound to take place and with the huge amount of money that was to be spent. I said that he would need an assistant. My suggestion was not followed.
Another suggestion that I made and urged on the government from time to time was that we should set up a defence expenditure committee, a committee that would continue to sit week by week and month by month for the purpose of scrutinizing expenditures, with the power of calling in the heads of the departments and of the different services, in order to check from time to time as to the methods that were being employed in the spending of the money and in the reorganization of the forces. That committee was not set up for two years. It has now been set up, but it was set up too late.
The minister now has an associate minister to take some of the load. You have that defence expenditure committee set up and probing what is termed waste and extravagance. In my opinion there should be a continuing committee of this house consisting of some of the members of the house who have had some experience in the services, and there are about 100 of them in the House of Commons. That kind of committee would have prevented from happening the kind of thing that brought about the Currie report. As to responsibility, the minister and his department are responsible for not taking the necessary precautionary steps which, in my opinion, could have prevented the bad tangle that was brought about and that

Supply-National Defence necessitated the bringing in of this famous Currie report.
The question arose as to whether it was right for Mr. Currie to make available to the deputy minister of national defence a copy of his report before it was tabled in the House of Commons. I do not think it was. I think that was a bad mistake. The way I see it is this. It is just as if, in civilian life, if someone commits a crime and the crown prosecutor prepares the case against him, he then submits the case to the accused to check it for accuracy as to whether or not it was properly prepared. That is about the correct analogy. It was the Department of National Defence that was under suspicion. They were being investigated and they were being charged. I think Mr. Currie will have to take the responsibility for releasing that report to those who were accused at that time. As to that particular angle, however, it is in the past as far as I am concerned; and I think what we must do from now on is to plan for the future.
I listened to the hon. member for Nanaimo speak on this question of Canada's present position in the matter of air defence. In "Canada's Defence Program" issued by the Minister of National Defence, on pages 1 and 5 I notice that he indicates that the department and the government are becoming conscious of the fact that our air defences in this country are not adequate. I never set myself up as an expert and I did not get to my feet here and try to tell the minister what he should do in that particular field; but I have always had the opinion that the building of a network of radar stations across this country was not enough. Of what value are those radar stations in the event of an air attack? We have nine squadrons of Sabre jets overseas at the present time and there is one squadron of Sabre jets in Canada. If something happened-and, as is indicated by this program the minister has shown us now, the only possible chance of attack on Canada would be from the air-we blow all the horns in Canada, and there is one squadron of Sabre jets in the country that may get somewhere fast enough to intercept somebody who might be coming in. I think that greater attention must be paid to that matter.
I also think-and I have thought it from the start-that sending foot troops or infantry over to Europe is a mistake. As far as Canada's defence is concerned, I believe that the main emphasis should have been put on the air force of this country and that there should be in Canada sufficient air force to protect this country in the event of something happening. In the second place, I think that the force that we should have in Europe is an armoured force. As to the soldier on 
foot today, may I say this. In the kind of situation that prevails over in Germany, there is in eastern Germany all kinds of heavy armour that could race through foot soldiers like nothing if it were desired. As far as we are concerned in Europe, I think the emphasis should be on heavy armour. I believe that our whole program in that regard has been wrong. I am glad to see that the minister and his department have done some thinking anyway in the matter of air defence; but I still think that it is necessary for them to give some thought to the problem of foot soldiers versus armour over in Europe.
Another thing that I never could see is the period of enlistment. You will take a soldier on for Korea, and he is enlisting in for eighteen months. He goes to Korea for eighteen months and you take him back and discharge him. You enlist him to go over with the 27th brigade. You equip him and train him and go to all that expense. He serves a year over in Europe with the 27th brigade, comes back and is discharged. In my opinion that system is all wrong. I believe that if a young man in this country is going to be persuaded to make a career of the service, periods of eighteen months and two years are too short. On the other hand, if we are going to get the young people of the right calibre in this country to make a career of the service, we must begin to understand that our defence program is not a short-term program and that it is not going to be handled by soldiers who go in for eighteen months and get out, go back in again for another year and go to Germany. They are merely Cook's tours.
I think something must be done to build up the morale of the army, and to establish the old esprit de corps that existed in the different units at the time of the first world war. One does not hear any praise today for the unit in which a soldier has been serving. They will say that they were in a year or eighteen months, and that they got out. The only comment we will hear about their service is that they had a pretty rough time of it, that they were not treated well, or that sort of thing.
Something must be done, as I say, to build up the morale of the army. I know that, under present circumstances, if I were 21 years of age and wished to join the armed services, I would want to join for a period of three years. I would want to be in long enough to find out something about it, and to determine whether or not I wanted to make a career of it. Because today in this country service in the armed forces is a good career for the average young man, and proper methods should be taken so that he will be

interested in the services and will want to make a career of it.
I have made a few notes on this question of morale in the services, and have set down what I think is wrong and what should be done. There are very few things as important to the armed services of a nation as morale. Whether morale is high or low can depend upon many factors-food, fair treatment, pay, discipline, the prompt and just redress of grievances, and so on. The methods by which discipline is administered, and the manner in which grievances are heard, are as important as any of these factors. Discipline, and the disposal of grievances of members of the armed services, are important not only because of their relationship to morale, but also because of necessary limitations of civil rights imposed upon those who join the forces.
Civil rights and privileges of a member of the armed services are very much restricted. He is subject to absolute discipline. He may not sue his sergeant if he thinks that he has been unjustly treated. He may not write letters to the editor complaining about his commanding officer. He may not stand up on a soap box and speak about the inefficient way in which his service is organized. His political rights are limited to little more than the privilege of voting. He may not form any organization remotely resembling a union. Indeed any attempt at mass redress of grievances is an offence, according to the military code. He has no say whatsoever in the formation or administration of the rules of military discipline by which he must abide.
For these reasons it is particularly important that parliament exercise the greatest vigilance to ensure that members of the armed forces are afforded the greatest possible protection, consistent with the requirements of military discipline and efficiency, to ensure that th'e possibility of injustice and wrong to members of the armed services is reduced to a minimum.
The National Defence Act passed by the House of Commons on June 7, 1950-and I was a member of the committee which looked it over-took away some of the limited protection which soldiers, sailors and airmen had under previous legislation. Formerly a soldier who felt himself wronged by his officer could appeal over the head of that officer to seek redress of his grievance. His right to carry his complaint right up as far as the general was established by law. Similarly, an officer who felt himself wronged or who had a grievance had the right of appealing over the heads of his superiors, ultimately to the King himself. Now, however, section 30 of the new act, instead of prescribing the right of the soldier with respect to redressing
Supply-National Defence wrongs, simply states that such rights and such procedure shall be as "prescribed in regulations made by the governor in council".
Again, the right of an accused person to be represented by counsel before court martial is not set out in the statute. Here again, the right to be represented at such proceedings is to be governed by "regulations made by the governor in council". This is provided by section 150 of the act.
Generally the new National Defence Act greatly increased the jurisdiction as well as the powers of punishment to be exercised by the various officers in the armed services. Previously any person convicted of insubordination was liable to penal servitude, or to a lesser punishment. Now, however, he is liable to life imprisonment or less. This provision is made in sections 74 and 75. The powers of a commanding officer were formerly limited to the awarding of 28 days' detention. Now his powers have been increased so that he may award 90 days' detention. This is set out in section 136.
These and numerous other examples may be cited to show how the armed services were, by the new act, made more authoritarian than previously and the rights of the members of the forces, as prescribed by law, were reduced. This tendency is to be deplored, and every effort should be made in parliament to afford the members of the services greater legal protection than they now have.
They have more protection than ever before, under the regulations.

I am simply setting out the sections of the act. Their rights were definitely laid down before the act was changed. Now they are subject to regulations; and who knows what those regulations are?
Another important element in maintaining morale in the armed services is pay. There is little doubt that in spite of increased pay in recent years there is a great deal of dissatisfaction with the rates now prevailing. The deputy minister of national defence in appearing before the House of Commons public accounts committee on May 3, 1951, admitted that one of the difficulties with respect to recruiting was that the men would receive less pay in the forces than they could get in industry.
During the war one of the social advances made by the armed services was the institution of dependents' allowances. These were paid for wives, children and other dependents, so that the income of a man with a large family was increased to help meet his greater needs. This provision went a long way toward recognizing a principle toward which socialists have strived for many years: "from
