Supply-National Defence each according to his ability, to each according to his need". Since the war the dependents' allowance has been greatly restricted so that now, while there is a flat marriage allowance, there is no provision for increases in the allowance according to the number of children, and no provision whatsoever for other dependents.
Officers in the three services have long complained about the requirement that they purchase their own dress uniforms and certain items of equipment. This requirement is a hangover from the old days when a career in the services was a privilege reserved for the well-to-do. A man had to have a private income of his own before he could afford to take out a commission in His Majesty's forces. Gradually this has been changed so that officers are properly paid for their jobs, but the requirement that they buy their own uniforms still remains. If service regulations require the wearing of particular uniforms or equipment, that equipment should be paid for by the service and not by the man concerned. Otherwise it is simply a roundabout way of reducing the officer's pay.
One of the biggest omissions in the attempt to build healthy morale among the armed services is the failure to provide the men with proper educational and informational services. The deputy minister of national defence admitted that if a man "goes into the infantry and remains with it, about the only skill that he would acquire would be some mechanical knowledge about the weapons with which he has to deal." The navy has educational officers to instruct recruits in academic subjects, but army and air force recruits must, if they wish to improve their educational background, take correspondence courses.
The complete failure of the services to provide proper informational and educational services for their men has led to a failure of the Canadian troops in Korea to appreciate the significance of the United Nations action there. Pierre Berton, the feature editor of Maclean's magazine, who visited Korea earlier this year, reported on his return that, while most of the officers know what they were fighting for, the men could seldom answer the question as to why they were there and what they were fighting for.
I have thought a lot about the morale of the troops in the services. We have heard many stories from Germany about the 27th brigade. Men have told me that the punishment meted out in that brigade was worse than anything they had seen during the last war, in which some of these boys had served for five years. They said it was no trouble


at all to get 90 days for the slightest misdemeanour. But there was one thing that stood out in their minds. When you were sentenced, even if it were only to 14 days' detention, the first thing that happened was that you were marched off to a German civilian barber who shaved off all your hair just like a convict. When you came back to your unit after the 14 days you still bore the stigma of a convict by having had your hair shaved off.
That kind of thing is ridiculous; it is absolute nonsense.
Another mistake made by the Department of National Defence is in connection with young men of 19 or 20 years of age who are taken into the service when married and perhaps with a child or two. These men are sent out of the country but their wives are not entitled to any allowance until they reach 21 years of age. Those women are left for a year or two without any allowance except what their husbands can spare by way of pay assignments.
I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that in building up an army, navy or air force he is dealing with human beings who react to injustices and the kind of thing I have just been talking about exactly as the minister or I would. It is not hard to be fair and reasonable with these young men, who are prepared to leave good jobs in many cases in order to make a contribution which they feel is vital under present world conditions.
I should like to say just a word on the matter of production. This is all-important. The hon. member for Nanaimo mentioned that our whole program was lagging, that we were not getting the kind of production we should. That may not be the fault of the Department of National Defence. I have in my hand a copy of a speech delivered by Mr. ' R. M. Brophy, deputy minister of defence production at the annual meeting of the Canadian industrial preparedness association in Quebec city on Thursday, October 16, 1952. I have had this for some time but I was struck with two passages which seem to indicate that there are others in this country who are not pulling their weight. I quote from page 8 as follows:
It is always a good thing to plan well in advance for a possible contingency but in doing so we don't want to neglect the job in hand. From the government's point of view, the task immediately ahead of us is to maintain production schedules and to get deliveries as quickly as possible in order to attain the degree of strength needed to stop aggression.
I well remember the enthusiasm which Canadian industry first showed in tackling this defence job. Much of that enthusiasm is still in evidence and there are many companies today that are putting their best effort into defence work. On the other

hand, we are facing situations where it is hard to get firms to take on certain types of defence contracts and also where there is a slowing down on work already in production. In other words, it seems to those of us who are looking at the picture from the government side, that there is a growing tendency to put priority on commercial work instead of defence contracts.
Then on page 11 he supplements that statement with these words:
Getting back to this matter of a certain indifference towards defence work that we are finding in industry, I want to point out again that this by no means applies to industry as a whole. However, it is true of certain firms. I am sure that we all embarked on this defence effort with the earnest desire to make a worth-while contribution to the defence of this country, and to the defence of the free world. I know that the delays and complexities have been discouraging. Nevertheless, the necessity to complete the program as soon as possible is still there. We have undertaken certain commitments and it is up to us to carry them through. As I see it, a defence contract carries with it a good deal of responsibility-responsibility to keep costs down, to maintain production schedules, and to meet delivery dates.
The financial inducement to accept this responsibility is, I know, not very great, but surely the returns are immeasurable. Individually, Canadians are making their contribution to Canada's defence. Industry, particularly in a free enterprise country, has an equal stake in this endeavour and the acceptance of defence contracts, even if they are not as lucrative as commercial business, is not too high a price to pay for the maintenance of political and economic freedom.
I think that answers the question of retarded production. It is the sort of story that we have been hearing since 1944, that certain industrial plants are reluctant to change over and retool for defence contracts. In those days there was a lot of stalling and delay. As the hon. member for Nanaimo suggests, there has been delay and there have been bottlenecks, but I would not hold the Department of National Defence responsible for that. The same thing happened when Great Britain had her back to the wall at Dunkirk. At that time the 5 per cent limitation on profits which had been laid down by statute by the House of Commons had to be removed. The minister of munitions and supply indicated to the house at that time that he could not get firms in this country to accept war contracts until the profits limitation had been removed. Those who were in business for the sake of business apparently did not have much patriotism or did not recognize the necessity of making a contribution toward defence. They were not ready to lose money by retooling for defence contracts.
Unless the government puts some teeth into some legislation these people will not carry their share of the load. The young man joining the air force to become a pilot may be giving up a job which pays him $500 a month. He leaves that job and risks his life because he realizes that this country is worth fighting
Supply-National Defence for. It is not too much to ask the man who wants to carry on commercially, who wants to make money out of his operations, to do something as well. I think the government ought to talk a little to people of that kind.
I want to say a few words about defence research. Suggestions have been made in this house that Canada should discontinue defence research, that we should sit back and let the United States do the necessary research work and take whatever they may get. In the meantime we would not be spending money on research.
That is a pretty immature attitude for any hon. member of this house to take in the kind of world that we are living in today and with the kind of defence that must be visualized for the future. Our defence set-up will come mainly from the test tubes of the scientists. Where would our whole defence program be without the atomic research and plant that we have today? There must be continuing research into defence against atomic attack. If you do not spend money on that type of defence you will not have much in the way of defence.
On the other hand, we are experimenting up in the north country, where there is extremely cold weather, on the use of equipment, machines, planes and so on. We are doing research on clothing to enable our troops to move in that kind of climate in the event of having to meet a threat that might come over the Bering sea. That kind of research has got to continue. I have in my hand a little booklet put out by the defence research board. Its title is "Research Opportunities". I am not going to take the time of the house to read from it, but if anyone who is thinking in terms of depending only on research that may be done in the United States will take the trouble to take a look at the kind of work that the defence research board is carrying on and relate it to any war that may occur in the future he will realize that the most important part of otir defence expenditure is the work that the scientists are doing in developing new machines, new equipment, new engines, further uses for atomic energy and all that kind of thing.
Actually in my opinion we are in the hands of the scientists for all of our defences in the future. I wanted to say that because I think anyone who makes the statement that Canada should discontinue defence research has not thought the matter through very far. That is about all I want to say. What I have said I thought should be said. As I said when I began, I do not set myself up as an expert. I think most members of the house are just feeling their way. In my judgment there are no experts on the world of the future in so far as war and

It is going to be a matter of trial and error from now on, but the least any of us can do is to try to think the thing through sanely and honestly and make the best contribution we can to our country regardless of what political tag we may wear.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I should like to join the hon. member for Nanaimo and the minister in paying tribute to the members of our armed forces. They have built up an enviable reputation throughout the years and have certainly served with distinction in the wars in which they have taken part. They are well known for their abilities, courage and resourcefulness in the field. We have been critical many times in the past and probably will be in the future but those criticisms have never been aimed at the armed forces as such. They have been criticisms of the department and the manner in which the administration of the armed services has been carried out.
In the present situation we know that things are serious. We are engaged now in a battle-and whether it be a hot war or a cold war it is still a battle-to maintain our way of life. This is not a war as we have known wars in the past. It is not a war between countries for trade benefits or anything of that sort. It is a battle between communism and the democratic way of life. We must never allow the peace overtures emanating from the communist bloc at the present time to lull us into a false sense of security. World domination has always been a part of communist doctrine. We sincerely hope that the peace moves that we have seen in the last few weeks are sincere. I am sure that Canada and the other western nations will meet the communists half way if they are sincere and will do all they can to bring about a lasting peace.
There is the possibility of course that the new soviet administration has seen the light and realizes that a world union based on power or anything of that sort will not work but that the community of nations upon this earth can get along peacefully if good will is exercised on the part of all. Although, as I indicated a few moments ago, we have always supported the expenditures of the Department of National Defence because we feel that at the present time defence is the most important branch of our government, we have been critical of the way in which the moneys have been spent at times and still are. The aims of the department are
[Mr. Gillis.l

certainly worthy but in many cases the results leave very much to be desired.
The minister said today that our commitments to NATO will be met. I am glad to learn that but I am not too sure that the NATO aims are high enough. I believe that the NATO objective for armed forces is something like 90 divisions or 1,350,000 men by 1954. If we achieve that we will have done something, but we are far from having enough available men to even fight against the might of soviet Russia for a short time until we can build up further defences. As General Gruenther said last year-these figures were placed on Hansard during this same debate of last year-the soviet active force consists of 175 divisions or something over 4 million men, and they also have 20,000 first-line aircraft and 300 submarines. These figures are out of date. He also pointed out that the East German police force has at the present time 360,000 men who could be converted into an army on very short notice. Coupled with at least
360,000	Russian soldiers in East Germany, it makes quite a formidable force to meet if they should decide to march across the border anywhere within Germany.
The magazine Aviation Age says that the 1951 Russian production was 10,700 fighter planes, 530 reconnaissance planes, 3,060 light and medium bombers, 1,430 transport aircraft and 5,000 trainers and liaison aircraft. During the same period the United States produced only 5,000 planes of all types and in the neighbourhood of 20,000 aircraft engines. It is quite apparent that at the present time soviet Russia exceeds us in air power, manpower and sea power. If they can keep on producing at this rate we can never catch up with them.
I should like to say a few words with regard to aircraft. General Hoyt Vandenberg was reported to have said that the MIG-15 is a better climber than the F-86 and that the F-86 has a longer range. At altitudes up to 25,000 feet the F-86 equals the speed and appears to handle better than the MIG-15. Above 25,000 feet the MIG is faster and has a higher service ceiling. He goes on to say that the MIG and the F-86 are roughly in the same general area of technical development.
However, we must remember that the MIG-15 is not the best fighter plane the Russians have. The MIG-19 and the LA-17 are both superior to the MIG-15 in all respects; and it is claimed that both are either in production or could be put into production in a very short period of time. It has been pointed out to us that our F-86's have proven themselves superior in many respects in

Korea, although we have had reports to the contrary. We have no way of knowing, however, whether the MIG-15's that are in use there are the Russians' first-line aircraft or whether they are a second-grade aircraft being shoved into the Korean war.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, I urged that the Department of National Defence consider building more small aircraft carriers. At that time I indicated that I was not referring to the Magnificent or anything like it, but to something of the order of the old converted merchant vessel aircraft carriers we had for escort purposes during the war. Certainly those aircraft carriers played a leading role in the defeat of the U-boats in the Atlantic during the last war. That was particularly due to the fact that while our escort vessels were unable to match the speed of many of the new submarines which the Germans then had, the aircraft, which incidentally were of an obsolete type, were able to make up the deficiency in speed. I would suggest to the minister that this type of aircraft carrier is cheap, and they would certainly pay for themselves in a very short time in the event of submarine attacks in the Atlantic.
The minister mentioned today that we have at the present time 56 ships in the R.C.N. I wonder just how many of those are first-line ships or how many would be any good under actual combat conditions and against modern submarines. 1 certainly hope they would be good; but if they are anything like the old ones, and if they have not been remodelled, they certainly would not stand up under modem warfare.
It is all right, Mr. Chairman, for the minister to say that our commitments to NATO will be met, but we must remember that while we are meeting these commitments we must have something left over for our own defence here at home. We must have fighter strength spread across this country so we can offset any air attack which might come to any part of the country. I believe the minister said, or it was said in the white paper that was tabled, that air attack would be the type of attack we would have to worry about here at home. Also I think we need an adequate mobile army defence force which can be transported in a hurry to any part of the country where it may be needed. We should have sufficient numbers to do some good when they get there-at least sufficient to hold back any invader until some of the NATO countries, the United States or someone else, can come to our assistance.
We certainly appreciate the troubles which the Minister of National Defence and the Department of National Defence have had in
Supply-National Defence the past, but I do not think these difficulties which have been pointed out should be sufficient to stop our defence effort. Our freedom, our way of life, and as a matter of fact our very lives are at stake. With good administration, conscientious defence spending, and with armed forces personnel of the type we have here in Canada we should be able to hold back all comers. We have the personnel, we have the ability, and now it is up to the department to see that we have those things which the men require to fulfil their duties to NATO and to us.

Mr. Chairman, this morning the minister spoke at some length of the quality and achievements of the fighting men of the army, navy and air force who have been taking an active part in the war in Korea. I should like to join with him in paying tribute to those men-tribute to their spirit, to the efficiency of their training, to their leadership and to their accomplishments. I was glad to hear the minister pay that tribute to the men who are out on the sharp edge as far as the defence of Canada is concerned at the present time. In that way I would hope to draw the attention of the general public to the work which they have been doing in defending all of us.
I was rather sorry, however, that the minister conveyed the general impression, I thought, that the efficiency, the spirit and the accomplishment of these men were due to a high level of efficiency as far as the Department of National Defence is concerned. I do not think that follows at all. The ability of the Canadian fighting man has been well demonstrated in every engagement in which he has taken part; and the job these men have done is, I think, essentially due to that ability.
I was also glad to hear the minister say something about the College Militaire Royal de Saint-Jean this morning. Perhaps I might say that I have a certain amount of personal knowledge in regard to the college because I have a boy attending there. I think at that college they are doing an excellent job from the point of view of training young Canadians both in the way of a general education and of giving them military training at the same time. They are also helping to foster a spirit of unity between the two chief races in Canada.
I have been at the college on two or three occasions and I was extremely favourably impressed with the commandant, Colonel Lahaie, and the way he is carrying on his job there. I did not have an opportunity of meeting many of his staff, but those whom I did meet also made a very favourable
3828	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence impression. I think the creation of this college will serve a very important need, one which has not been met before in Canada, and will considerably strengthen the country from both points of view I have just mentioned.
As has already been indicated by the hon. member for Nanaimo, the objectives of our national defence effort were stated in the white paper of, I think, three years ago. They are again stated in the white paper which was issued yesterday. I shall not read them but they are, briefly, to defend Canada itself, to meet our commitments overseas-our commitments to the United Nations or NATO- and organization to build up strength in the event that total war should break out.
With those objectives I am in full agreement as, I believe, is every loyal citizen of Canada. My criticism of the government is of the way in which they have attempted to attain these objectives or, perhaps I should say, how they have failed to reach them effectively. In that failure they have wasted large sums of the taxpayers' money.
For the past five years I have condemned the government on the grounds that our effective fighting forces are very small in comparison with the amount we have been paying for them. Unfortunately, year by year this situation has grown worse instead of better. If we look at the figures which are given on page 86 of the report of the Department of National Defence for 1952, and also in the white paper at page 36, we get a picture of how the cost has mounted. If these are arranged in the form of a table, as I have them here, the thing strikes one quite forcibly. For 1949-50 we had in the active forces 47,185 personnel; the cost was $384,879,000-I shall not give the odd dollars. This works out at a cost per man in uniform of $8,157. In 1950-51 there were 68,427 personnel; the cost was $782,457,000, and the cost per man was $11,435. In 1951-52 the total personnel was 95,394; the cost was $1,415,473,000, and the cost per man, $14,438. In 1952-53 the total personnel was 104,486; the cost was $1,889,507,000, and the cost per man, $18,083. For this year the estimated cost as given in the white paper is $2,243,767,000. We do not know the number of personnel, so we cannot make that calculation.
Based on the figures we have for these four years, we find the cost per man mounting from $8,100 to $11,400, to $14,400 and to $18,000. In other words there has been a steady progression upward in the cost per man in uniform. I might point out also that the strengths I have taken here are the strengths given for the end of the year in each case, that is at March 31. If one took
rMr. Harkness.]

the average strength throughout the year the figure would be somewhere halfway between each of the figures I have given, and therefore the cost per man would be considerably greater than the amounts I have given.
Now, these figures show how the cost has mounted for each man and woman in uniform. Of the 104,000 men and women we now have in the services, a large number are in administrative or training positions. The number actually in fighting units and capable of being put into battle is, of course, very much smaller. According to the figures on page 15 of this white paper the total number of men in fighting formations or units is 43,200. That would include a considerable number of non-fighting personnel, such as medical personnel and so forth. I would estimate that not more than 35,000 or 40,000 actual fighting personnel are to be found there.
This morning the minister said that we now have a larger proportion of troops operational than we had three years ago, and that is correct. He went on to say that the number we now have operational compares very favourably with other countries. I would have accepted that more readily if it had not been exactly the same answer he gave two or three years ago when I brought up this question. At that time he stated that the number of operational troops we had, as compared with non-operational troops, compared favourably to the number in any other country. Today he says we have greatly increased the number of operational troops, so surely there is a discrepancy there. It leads one to wonder about the minister's statement.
In any event we have a comparatively small number of fighting troops ready to go into action. As I say, probably 35,000 or
40,000	are in this category. In order to secure this comparatively small fighting potential we will have spent in the five years from 1949 to 1954, a total of $6,720,084,000. This is the total of the figures I gave before. I should like to ask, Mr. Chairman, can this showing be defended by the government as efficient handling of defence funds when we have spent such enormous amounts for, comparatively speaking, such small effective fighting formations? Of course the minister will say that a large part of this sum has been spent for armaments, ships, airplanes, guns, for buildings, the stockpiling of equipment and things of that sort. It is true that large amounts have been spent for these purposes, but the unfortunate fact is ' that even the small forces we have in being are not fully equipped with up-to-date arms. At the same time, I must say that we have more carpets,

neckties, teapots and things of that kind than these forces will be able to use in a good many years.
Last year I pointed out that we now have considerably fewer field and anti-tank guns, rifles and small arms of all sorts than we had four years ago, in spite of having made some purchases of United States type arms of these kinds. We have shipped equipment of that sort for some three divisions or more to Europe. We are, therefore, in the position of having spent this very large amount, yet we have a smaller amount of equipment in many lines on hand for fighting purposes than we had four years before the program started. We have also only a small number of up-to-date tanks, of the Centurion type. We have fewer serviceable vehicles of all sorts than we had four years ago. When we come to the air force, on which a large measure of the expenditure has been made, we find that, according to the white paper and the minister's statement, we now have nine squadrons of F-86E Sabre jets in operation. These are the only operational squadrons of up-to-date aircraft which we have. There are three more squadrons of these Sabres in the process of formation and training in Canada.
We have, however, no fully operational squadron of CF- 100's, the aircraft that has been announced as the one to provide for the defence of Canada itself. The white paper says there is one squadron of CF-lOO's but that squadron is only in the process of formation. I know it is not fully operational. In addition to that, of course, the Minister of Defence Production announced a short time ago that the total number of CF-lOO's of all sorts produced to date was 16. The Minister of National Defence made some statement to the effect that they had deliberately let the program lag to some extent, but that certainly was not the tenor of the statement he made last year in connection with the CF-100, or the year before that. These aircraft were supposed to be available in large numbers long before this, and in the sky ready to defend this country. We have not got them.
We have been told that we have a partially constructed radar screen, but we do not know how complete it is. One thing we do know is that we have practically nothing with which to back up that screen, either in the way of fighter aircraft or ack-ack defence. As the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out, a radar screen is useless for defence purposes unless you have something with which to back it up. He referred to the statement made by Wing Commander Rohmer; and I too think he did a great service in drawing
Supply-National Defence that fact to the general attention of the people of Canada. It is a matter which we have raised year after year, but I am afraid it did not sink into the consciousness of a great many of the Canadian general public that we were comparatively defenseless as far as any air attack from the north was concerned.
The minister also mentioned the airborne brigade. That airborne brigade, of course, has been changed around considerably because of the rotation system of troops to Korea and so forth. However, whatever its efficiency may be-and I believe and trust that it is quite high again, because the people now in the airborne brigade have had upwards of a year of training in that role- and whatever the quality of the airborne brigade may be, it would not be of a great deal of use in discharging its function of being dropped to meet any attempted invasion of this country from the north, or the seizure of an airfield in the north so that bombing could be carried on down here or anything of that sort, because we simply have not the transport planes to carry it and drop it there. To that extent the airborne brigade serves only to lull the people of Canada into a false sense of security. For that brigade to be effective we must have planes ready to take them where they are needed and drop them there; but we just have not those planes.
What all this adds up to, Mr. Chairman, is that we have not the requirements to meet our primary objective, namely the defence of Canadian territory. In other words that objective has not been met, and it has not been nearly met. When we come to the second commitment, namely our obligations to UN and NATO, the minister says that has been met or will be met by the target date. We have done considerably better in meeting that objective than we have in meeting the primary one. When we come to the third objective, we find it is to a large extent a matter of the reserve forces and the general organization that is to be built up; and I shall deal with that matter later.
The small amount of defensive strength that we have in relation to the amount we have spent is also shown up clearly by a comparison of the numbers of personnel in the forces now and their cost, with the numbers and costs during the war. This comparison shows to what a great extent the cost per man in the services has increased. The increase is really out of all proportion to what one could reasonably expect. These figures are to be found at page 86 of the report of the Department of National Defence. I have already put on the record the figures for the past four or five years and I should

Supply-National Defence now like to refer to the figures for the years 1941 down to 1945.
In the year 1941-42 there were in our active forces approximately 426,000 personnel and the expenditure was $1,011,451,000, or a cost of $2,373 per man. In 1942-43 the number in the forces was 640,592 and the cost was $1,865,622,000, or a cost per man of $2,912. In 1943-44 there were in the services 709,666 personnel and the expenditure was $2,629,094,000, or a cost per man of $3,704. This was the year in which our forces were at their height, and this was the year in which we started to fight in earnest. In spite of that fact, when we were blowing away large amounts of ammunition, and when we had the largest number of people in uniform that we had at any time during the war, the cost was only $3,704 per man whereas today it is approximately $18,000. In 1944-45 the number in the forces was 672,632 and the expenditure was $2,938,377,000 or a cost per person of $4,369.
Compare those costs, namely $2,300, $2,900, $3,700 and $4,300 at the height of the war, when the greatest expenditures of all were taking place, with the cost during the last three or four years of $8,100, $11,400, $14,800 and $18,000, with the figure still to go up in the next year, apparently. It certainly indicates that something in the nature of extravagance has been going on.
The minister, of course, may say that the costs now are greatly increased over what they were during the war, and that the general cost of living has increased. That is true, of course. But what he should add, but will not, is that that fact again is, to a considerable extent, owing to the policy of this government as a result of which we now have a 50-cent dollar. But even if you take that fact into consideration and allow that general costs of everything now are twice what they were, we still find that defence costs per man are over four times what they were at the height of the war, or just twice as much as we might reasonably expect them to be.
Amongst the chief reasons, for this excessive cost are poor administration, overblown staffs, inefficiency, extravagance and waste. The Auditor General's report, the Currie report, and the two reports which we were not permitted to see all show these conditions to exist in certain branches of the defence department. I think no reasonable person in Canada is in any doubt that similar conditions prevail to a greater or lesser degree in all branches. The reports, of course, dealt especially with inefficiency, extravagance and waste. I have spoken on those matters in


a previous debate and I shall not go into them again at this moment. However, I should like to look at the matter of how staffs have been expanded, or in other words the empire-building which has gone on in the Department of National Defence.
A return which was recently brought down for the hon. member for Kamloops showed that in the deputy minister's office there are now more personnel than there were at any time during the war. What is or can be the justification for a state of affairs of that sort? If we look at the estimates for this year we find, under departmental administration alone, that the number of employees has increased from 2,512 in 1952-53 to 3,599 for 1953-54, or an increase of 1,087 in one year. If we go back and look at the estimates for the previous year we find that in 1951-52 the number of these civilian employees was 1,230. So there was an increase of 1,282 the previous year. The staff was more than doubled for the next year, in order to bring the figure up to 2,512 in these estimates for 1952-53. Well, this leads one to ask where this thing is going to stop. Are they going to keep on multiplying and multiplying and multiplying these staffs, until they employ half the people in Canada?
Then the number of civilian employees throughout the department showed a very sharp rise, though perhaps not quite as bad as in the departmental administration branch. Throughout the whole department in 1952 there were 21,782 civilian employees. For 1953-54 that figure is up to 26,638, or an increase of 4,856. And I would add that these figures do not include the casual and prevailing rate employees, who must number several thousand, although the exact number is not given.
One of the particular spots where the increase in the number of civilian employees is shown is in connection with stenographers and typists. Evidently the paper war has been and is being stepped up, although we were told last year, I believe it was, that the paper work in the department was to be simplified. Well, I can readily believe that paper is flowing more freely than ever both into and out of national defence headquarters, because I have seen some graphic examples of it. My route home from this building often takes me between the national defence headquarters buildings, and on several occasions I have seen large burlap bundles filled with paper. Evidently this is waste paper that has been piled ready to be taken away. It is an arresting example of the vast number of pamphlets, forms and letters which have to be thrown out frequently, and gives one some idea of the enormous amount

of paper that this very large number of civilian employees are kept busy passing about from one to another. The cost of the staff employed in shuffling this paper about is enormous. Even the cost of the paper must be very high.
Then last year I spoke at some length concerning the multiplication of staffs that has taken place at national defence headquarters, as well as at command and area headquarters, and at similar headquarters of other services. I shall not repeat what I said at that time, except to mention that in one branch of national defence headquarters alone, that of the army training and staff duties branch, there are now seven full colonels, each with a staff of officers and other ranks, as well as civilians. All those people are doing the work accomplished before the war by one colonel, three majors, and something like twelve other ranks.
No doubt the amount of work has increased; but I doubt very much whether, so far as that particular branch is concerned, the amount of work has more than doubled, or anything along that line. As I said last year, they have to put out the same number of training pamphlets whether they have a thousand men or ten thousand men. The work of preparing those pamphlets is the same in either case. But in any event we see this enormous multiplication of effort taking place, a great deal of which I am sure does not contribute very greatly to the defence of this country, and which is certainly very expensive.
Then, extremely large sums of money have been spent for equipment, but we have received comparatively little information as to what equipment we have received for these large sums of money. Last year in the defence expenditure committee there was discussion of an item of $683 million for aircraft, about which we could get practically no information. We find in these estimates another $400 million for aircraft. I would hope that this year, when we begin to discuss the estimates in detail, the minister will be able to give us a considerable amount of information as to how this billion-dollar item has been spent. What have we to show for it? What did we receivfe for it? So far as we know, all we have is nine squadrons of Sabre fighters, plus a certain number of training aircraft.
The same applies in respect of equipment for the army. Large sums of money have been spent for it, and from the last information we were able to get in last year's defence expenditure committee, it did not appear that much equipment had been secured. In fact a very limited amount had
Supply-National Defence been secured at that time. That is another matter upon which we should have more detailed information from the minister during the discussion of his estimates.
The minister said that, so far as administrative procedures and things of that nature were concerned, standardization had gone ahead satisfactorily, but that it had not worked out so well in respect of arms. He expressed the hope that a standard rifle would be adopted in the not too distant future. I firmly believe that the decision made three years ago by the minister to standardize our arms with those of the Americans was a very grave mistake. After the decision was made, the department started in on the program of getting rid of the arms we then had by sending them to European nations. Then the department found that in many cases they could not get arms from the Americans, and that when they did they were not as satisfactory as the ones they could get from the British.
That program had to be halted, and it definitely was halted. Only a limited number of American small arms, guns and the like were purchased. Practically no purchases were made of United States tanks. I believe the mistake then made has done a great deal to increase the expense of our defence effort, and has greatly complicated it and made it less efficient than otherwise it would have been.
I suggest the minister should tell us what amount of United States armament we now have, including small arms, guns and the like. He should tell us what Canadian forces, if any, are equipped with these small arms, in other words to what units they have been issued. The minister said-and I am not sure whether it was in his speech or in the white paper

that good progress has been made in producing 105-millimeter and 155-millimeter guns. I would like to know how many of these guns have been produced, and what units in our forces are equipped with them; because we were definitely short of guns, due to the number that were shipped to Europe.
I should like now to say a word about the reserve army. Once again I would compliment the members of our reserve army, those men who give so much of their time and energy in an attempt to keep the reserve in force. I would include not only those men, but also members of the naval reserve and of the air force reserve. These are men who are devoted to their task but who, to a very large extent, are not supported to the extent they should be-and indeed never have received the support from this government that should have been given. At page 14 of
Is it not a good thing to begin at the base, to show the increase from the base?

I think it is a good thing if the impression the minister is trying to make is that everything is improving with the Canadian defence forces, but I do not think it is a good thing to try to deceive the Canadian people and make them believe that things have been improving constantly when as a matter of fact they have been standing still for the last few years. The reserve forces have been hard put to it to maintain the strength they have.

The situation in the reserve forces has not been good. There is no question about that. Along with other hon. members I have been receiving an increasing number of complaints from men in the reserve forces. The general situation in a lot of the reserve units is pretty well summarized in an article which appeared in the Calgary Herald of March 30. This was written by Jim Senter, who was a member of the unit I was in overseas and also of the reserve force unit which I commanded after the war. This was an artillery unit, and therefore I think he knows what he is talking about. I believe he is still in the reserve army. The article goes on in this way:
Officers Claim Faults Injuring Reserve Army Lack
of Understanding and Scarcity of Equipment Cited as Main Troubles
A lack of understanding, a shortage of permanent and non-permanent personnel and a scarcity of good, modern technical equipment is tearing the heart out of Canada's reserve army.
And then again:
In part, at least, the reasons for the above situation are not too hard to find. These are: Overcommitment of Canada's small, but efficient regular army, now charged with the defence of Canada and the maintaining of two brigades for service under United Nations charter in Germany and Korea; and, promises and shipments of Canadian army equipment to countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization have stripped stores and supplies for the reserve army.
"I think they are making a big mistake", said one officer. "Most of our equipment was hauled away gradually and what we have left is becoming obsolete fast. At this rate things are going to be just like they were in 1939-40 when the artillery was training on 18-pounders and 4-5-inch howitzers.
"If a third great war should come, troops would require so much training after the outbreak that it would be years before they would be ready to fight."
This officer suggested that at least one piece of each item of modern equipment should be issued reserve army units "so we can keep up to date. They keep promising us that equipment will be replaced but, at the present rate, that's going to take years and it will be obsolete by the time we get it."
Particular shortages are to be found in transport, technical survey equipment such as the director, so important in artillery work, and range tables, without which artillery batteries can scarcely function.
The infantry in Calgary is not too badly off, but artillery units are in the ridiculous position of training with guns without breech rings. The director shortage is reminiscent of pre-second great war days when units made do with wax tins and broom sticks.
The article says the infantry is not too badly off, but I was talking to some infantry officers when I was home over Easter and they were complaining bitterly about shortages of equipment. They told me their carriers were about to be taken away from them. They told me their carrier platoon was the best they had. Their jeeps have gone already, and other pa'rts of their transport are gone. Their contention was that if their carriers

were taken the only thing they would have left with which to train would be small arms, and generally the spirit of the battalion would suffer seriously as a result.
It is extremely difficult to understand why the equipment of the reserve forces should have been constantly drained away during the past four years. The minister gets up here year after year and says they are anxious to do everything possible for the reserve forces, yet we find this situation existing. This equipment is gradually being taken away from them, and as a result their efficiency has been destroyed.

The hon. member must know that the equipment to which he refers is being taken away to be rehabilitated and then shipped to Europe, and will be replaced by equipment of the latest type. That procedure is well under way.

What is the use of taking away equipment and saying that it will be replaced, and then months and months go by and it is not replaced. These people are left without equipment with which to train. How can you expect the spirit of a unit to be kept up; how can you keep up the interest of the men; how can you carry on training if you take equipment away and say that some time in the future they will be given more modern equipment? As a matter of fact the equipment they had should have been left with them until the modern equipment was available. Then they would have had something with which to train; but to take away this equipment and have months go by without it being replaced is the surest way I know to kill interest. The article continues:
We're not getting the understanding or co-operation we should from western command. They treat us as active force units. Returns, returns, returns, all the time.
It is the same paper war I was talking about a while ago.
It's impossible to do them all in the few hours' training time allotted each week.
I do not blame the western command for this situation. I blame national defence headquarters and the minister. They are the people who lay down what returns have to be sent in. They are the people responsible for the paper war that the reserve army has to fight. The western command or any other command merely carry out the orders they get from here.
This article goes on to deal with other matters and then makes a few recommendations as to how the situation might be improved. One of the suggestions made is one that I have mentioned before. This is the suggestion that a certain number of officers and N.C.O.'s from reserve units should
14, 1953
Supply-National Defence be sent on a tour of duty of six weeks or two months in Korea or Europe.
I have heard the minister say on several occasions that the availability of officers has always been a matter of worry, that there has been difficulty in getting officers. I would think that any deficiency which may exist in connection with officers and N.C.O.'s could readily be met by giving reserve force officers a tour of duty in Korea. Of course it would have to be limited in time because they have civilian jobs which they could not stay away from for very long. We have an airlift in operation. It would be quite a practical business to carry them back and forth, and the cost of doing so would be no greater than the cost of putting them in camps, sending them to schools and things of that sort which have proved comparatively ineffective. From the training point of view, if you adopted some scheme of this sort you would give these people the best training they could possibly have and make them very much more effective in their own units when they returned from such tours. You would also build up the reserve of people who had had actual experience in the Korean war about which the minister was talking. That is one way in which interest in the reserve forces and their standard of training could be improved, and I would recommend it very strongly to the minister.
Other ways, of course, are to reduce the number of returns and the great quantity of paper work involved which reserve force people on the whole just do not have the time to attend to. Another would be greater interest being displayed on the part of the government, national defence headquarters and so on in the reserve forces and their problems, particularly expressed in making sure that they have sufficient equipment. I have spoken about the matter of equipment before. Apparently equipment of all sorts is short. One of the things which the reserve force units resented particularly was the loss of their jeeps, which left them without vehicles to do all sorts of little jobs. I do not think you can expect anything else but that the reserve force officers will have to put up a terrific fight to keep their men and to get more men in the units and get them interested if they are constantly short of equipment, if what they have is taken away from them, and if they constantly have to improvise.
There is one other matter which I should like to mention briefly. I refer to promotions within the Royal Canadian Air Force. Last year I took up the matter of promotions of administrative officers with the minister and pointed out that the number of promotions

Supply-National Defence in that category had been very small. I understood there was a considerable amount of feeling among administrative officers because of that fact, which naturally did harm in the service. The minister made a reply which I thought was none too satisfactory.
However, there is another matter along the same line that I should like to take up. I asked some questions as to the length of time officers in the R.C.A.F. had been in their present ranks. I received a return on the 4th of March. The highest rank is air commodore, of whom there is only one, who has held that rank for over nine years. Taking all officers, there were 120 who had had no promotion for over nine years. There were 173 who had had no promotion for nine years. There were 298 who had had no promotion for over six years and 913 who had had no promotion for over three years. Many of these men are junior officers.
Taking flying officers, the lowest rank, there were 21 who had had no promotion for over nine years. There were 33 who had had no promotion for nine years, 98 who had had no promotion for over six years and 285 who had had no promotion for over three years. I should like to ask the minister to toe prepared to make a statement on the promotion policy of the R.C.A.F. particularly, and also of the army and navy. It seems to me that it is very difficult to get efficient service if you have considerable numbers of men, particularly in the two most junior ranks, who have had no promotion for nine years or more. It is bound to kill initiative and make things sticky as far as carrying out military activities of all sorts is concerned. It may be that there is a good explanation, I do not know; but certainly it is a matter about which the committee should have some explanation.

DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE Defence services-
241. To provide for the Canadian forces, the defence research board and other expenditures relating to defence, including contributions toward the military costs of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; to authorize expenditures in the current year out of the amount hereby provided, not exceeding $324,000,000, under the provisions of section 3 of the Defence Appropriation Act, 1950, and to provide that, notwithstanding subsection 3 of that section, where equipment or supplies acquired by the Canadian forces after March 31, 1950, are transferred, the estimated present value thereof shall, if the governor in council so directs, be credited to this vote instead of being paid into the special account mentioned in the said subsection 3, and when so credited may be expended for the purposes of the Canadian forces; and notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act to authorize total commitments for the foregoing purposes of $3,994,895,578 regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment (of which it is estimated that $1,971,926,275 will come due for payment in future years), $1,960,159,633.

Mr. Chairman, I do not suppose any member who heard the minister's statement this morning on Canada's defence program could have failed to be impressed with the thought that if the defences of Canada were in as good shape as the minister would have us take from his statement, there would not be very much for anybody to say about it. However, the facts of the situation are, Mr. Chairman, that unfortunately there are a number of us who feel that we cannot take that reassurance from the minister's statement; .because he has been making these reassuring


statements every year now, particularly since Korea and the inauguration of the three-year, $5 billion program.
The developments and the discoveries of what is going on in the department do not warrant us in relaxing our efforts or, I think it is fair to say, they do not warrant us in relaxing our criticism in an attempt to obtain a more realistic and efficient defence program in this country and, also, as part of the United Nations Organization and as a country having responsibilities to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
It is, of course, true that one of the main features with which our criticism deals is the actual amounts of money which are spent; but, Mr. Chairman, it should be made clear, if it has not already been made clear, that the objection on that score is not that we have to spend money on defence. Owing to the circumstances in which Canada and other free nations find themselves it is unfortunately necessary to provide for defence on a scale with which we have never before been confronted in a time of nominal peace. It is not the fact that the government is asking parliament to authorize huge sums of money for defence which is criticized but, rather, the fact that we are told that we are getting defence which is quite unrealistic when you compare the situation as it actually exists, and the adequacy of our defences, with what should be available in terms of real defence after the amount of money we have spent.
This attempt to have the house and the country believe that we have in fact got real defence for all of the money we have spent takes two forms. The first is with respect to the details of the program announced in the various white papers we have had, as to the size of our defence forces themselves, the efficiency of the various components and so on, to the effect that they are at a certain level of efficiency and that they have equipment. That does not seem to be the case when we analyse the situation. Second, there is an apparent belief-and certainly it is so consistently put forward by the department that it may be the minister believes it himself-that money spent on frills and fineries, on things which do not actually increase the shooting power of Canada's defence forces, nevertheless is providing a defence machine which will be adequate to discharge the job of defending Canada, when in fact the things for which large amounts of defence funds are being spent will not give us any defence at all in the real sense of the word.
In respect to the first of the unrealistic branches of the minister's defence of his own department-that is, that our defence forces are actually equipped and ready, that we have forces in being to an extent which does

not seem to be borne out by a detailed analysis of the situation-I think there cannot be a better example of the truth of what I have said than that which was furnished recently in the statement by Wing Commander Rohmer, which was previously referred to in this debate. Wing Commander Rohmer, in the speech he made on March 26, 1953, in Toronto, took exception to the very thing I have been mentioning, these general statements about the adequacy of the defence forces of Canada-statements which are not borne out by the facts. He opened his address with a statement or an article appearing in the press in Toronto which was obviously inspired by the department. He took objection to the statement contained in that article. We have all had similar experiences concerning inspired articles in the press with regard to what the government is doing. The words to which the minister took exception are the following:
Backed by R.C.A.F. jet fighter squadrons and the army's mobile striking force, they constitute a military force that experts say is capable of dealing with any Arctic invader.
Military authorities, guided by long years of experience, believe that control of the air is vital to any successful land attack on this continent.
With a fast striking air force to guard the northern skies, the mobile army striking force to deal with a surprise airborne invasion, and a fast-growing navy to patrol the coastal waters, Canada's home defences against attack are stronger today than ever before in peacetime.
Those words, Mr. Chairman, were found in a Toronto newspaper article on January 12, and they are words obviously inspired by the Department of National Defence.
What evidence has the hon. member of that?
I have the evidence of other similar articles.
That is no evidence at all.
Perhaps the minister is indicating that the department does not agree with this statement in the article I just read.
With what has just been said? That article goes much farther than the facts or than anything I have ever said.

Then the minister is saying that those words which appear in the press article-
With a fast striking air force to guard the northern skies, a mobile army striking force to deal with a surprise airborne invasion, and a fastgrowing navy to patrol the coastal waters, Canada's home defences against attack are stronger today than ever before in peacetime.
-are not based upon anything the minister has said, and do I understand him to say that it goes much farther than the facts?

I would have to sort it out. The final statement that the defence forces
Supply-National Defence available are much greater than ever before in peacetime is completely true, but that vast striking-
Fast, not vast.
There is a fast one, but I thought you said vast. I am sorry, but I did not make the statement. I have made lots of statements and I stand by them, but I did not make that statement.

I had not indicated that the minister made the statement, but I was saying we had experience with similar reports in the press which are said to be inspired by military experts or departmental officials. Then when we try to tie it down we cannot find the name of the expert who actually said it. I am glad to have the minister's statement. I will not go any farther than what he has actually said here. I understand now he says that this does not represent or is not based upon a statement made by the department, and that certain parts of the article go beyond anything which is justified by the facts or by any official statement made by the department.

I said that having understood the hon. member as saying "vast". Now that I have the correct impression as "fast", 1 would have to look at the article and sort out what was in accordance with what I said before and what was not.

Then we are left in the position that perhaps we had better wait until the minister deals with the matter at a later stage. On that basis, then, I should like to deal with a statement made by Wing Commander Rohmer to the effect that except for three Sabre squadrons under training to go to Europe under NATO, Canada could not put up a single modern aircraft. He said that Canada is absolutely defenseless against air attack, and after analysing the situation went on as follows:
Gentlemen, the air officer commanding, air defence command of the R.C.A.F., through no fault of his own or that of the R.C.A.F., could not stop one Russian bomber attacking over 30,000 feet in broad daylight, unless it stumbled into the Quebec area.
From other parts of that speech it is obvious that the reason he said "unless it stumbled into the Quebec area" is that it is in the Quebec area that the three Sabre squadrons destined to form part of Canada's air division of the NATO forces in Europe are at the present time. If they were to leave tomorrow the situation would be, on the basis of this article, that even if it did stumble into the Quebec area the R.C.A.F. could not stop one Russian bomber attacking at over 30,000 feet in broad daylight. This is

We find the same impression being created this year, that adequate attention is being given to home defence, by the statement on the first page of the white paper tabled yesterday. It reads:
There has also been a substantial Increase in the emphasis on the defence of North America against air attack.
On page 5 of the white paper we find this statement:
In the event of an all-out war the most probable method of attack upon the North American continent would be by air.
This statement is under the heading, "First objective: Defence against direct attack." As I say, Mr. Chairman, similar statements have been made year after year in this house and in the course of the white papers, yet we find the situation such that if tomorrow the three Sabre squadrons forming part of the NATO component were dispatched overseas, we could not stop one Russian bomber attacking at over 30,000 feet in broad daylight. We have other statements which have been made to the house in an effort to reassure the country that everything is as well as it could possibly be in the best of all possible departments. There have been statements to the effect that the aircraft production program is going ahead as scheduled; yet as a result of pressing for details we have a statement made by the Minister of Defence Production- with obvious signs of annoyance that he should have been pressed into giving that accounting-with respect to the production of CF-lOO's, that after four years and the expenditure of $130 million only 16 airframes and 96 engines had been produced up to December 31, 1952. After four years and the expenditure of $130 million of government funds, that is the situation.
Then we find another statement being made which, if taken at face value, would give the impression that Canada has a squadron now equipped with CF-lOO's, capable of taking to the air. Of course the fact is that, although the squadron has now been activated, it is not yet in a position to take to the air and operate as a fighting unit. Here is what the white paper says, again at page 5:
The first regular squadron equipped with CF-100 all-weather, twin-engine, jet fighters, was recently formed-
It is not much use forming a squadron unless it is in a position to fly and fight. I do not know why, in these white papers, the


minister does not complete that side of the picture. We find that that sort of completed statement is never made. We are left with the indefinite and vague information that by the end of the fiscal year a number of these squadrons will be operating. But we have the information, which was made available finally by the Minister of Defence Production, that in the field of air defence with respect to the CF-100-which we have been told is the one aircraft on which we can rely to meet the requirements of defence of Canada's northland-after four years, the expenditure of $130 million, and vast numbers of promises, all we had received up to December 31, 1952 were 16 airframes and 96 engines.
Then we were told'-and the minister spent some time this morning in entering this branch of his defence-that we have spent vast sums of money on defence. But I should think that fully half of the minister's lengthy statement this morning was devoted to an outline of the purchase of objects and of installations which would not in fact stop one Russian from attacking Canada. Neither the Russians nor any other enemy would be deterred by any amount of defence building or construction of the sort which the minister was taking obvious pride in outlining to us this morning. We are not going to stop the Russians by building barracks or indeed by building airfields unless we have the aircraft to operate from those airfields. We are not going to stop them by building barracks to accommodate the soldiers who form part of the airborne brigade unless we also have the aircraft to lift that brigade and the places to set them down in the areas in which it is anticipated that the Russians may be making their first landing.
The building of barracks and training grounds is not going to be the thing which will stop a Russian attack. What will stop a Russian attack will be a trained and equipped group which is not only ready with its own weapons but is capable of being moved to the places where the attack is anticipated. So far as one can find from the white paper or from the minister's statement this morning, we do not have that airborne brigade in being in that sense, even at the end of two-thirds of the $5 billion, three-year defence program. But we have vain statements-that is to say vain in the sense that they are not going to help us to repel a potential attacker-as to the amounts that we have been spending on construction.
We were told by the minister this morning that the construction program calls for $358 million this year. Then we were told-and it was said in a manner which indicated pride and satisfaction on the part of the minister-

that this amount was more than twice that expended during the peak of wartime construction. That is a most extraordinary thing for the minister to take pride in, Mr. Chairman. In wartime, in the last war, we had approximately 1 million men under arms. Yet this year, although we have only 104,000 in the three forces, or only about one-ninth or one-eighth of what we had at the peak of the wartime, we are spending more than twice what we spent on construction in the peak wartime year.
This fact that we are spending on construction more than twice what was spent in the peak war year is put forward as an important aspect of the defence program, as though somehow or another it was going to deter a potential aggressor. I should think that, on the contrary, a potential aggressor, if he had any aggressive intent, would be encouraged to think that the government of Canada in this year, with about one-ninth of the number of men in uniform that it had in the war, was spending with respect to the forces over twice as much on construction as it spent in the peak war year, instead of getting on with the job or providing them with the necessary arms, equipment and aircraft to enable them to do the job for which they were designed.
Then the minister appeared to take pride in putting forward as a defence of the defence effort the fact that the department, on this type of construction or on the acquisition of this type of installation, has spent more than twice as much-and done so in one-tenth the time-as the Canadian National Railways has spent in the whole course of its existence. What an extraordinary and perfectly meaningless argument to put forward as a defence of the way in which the government is discharging its responsibility to provide for the defence of Canada against aggression. All one can say there, Mr. Chairman, is that perhaps the country has rather more to show from what the Canadian National Railways has spent, even though it may have taken ten times as long to spend it, than we shall have as a real contribution to defence from the type of things in this field for which the government is spending these vast sums of money.
Then the minister seemed to take much pleasure out of the fact that somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2 billion out of a total of $5 billion was to be spent on construction-
I think he used the general word "construction"-or under the heading of construction. Was that not approximately the figure he used this morning?

No. Speaking from memory I think the figure on construction was $665 million. I think the $2 billion was for equipment.

The minister says $665 million will be spent on construction. That will be approximately one-eighth of the total of $5 billion to be spent on defence in this three-year period. That fact seemed to give the minister a good deal of satisfaction and to be regarded by him as an argument that the government must be discharging adequately its responsibility in this field of providing defence because it was going to spend on construction one-eighth of the total cost of the defence effort. Mr. Chairman, you would almost think that Canada, during the war of 1939-45, made no more contribution to the war effort than a country the size of, let us say, Luxembourg. You would almost think we did not have any accommodation at all in which to train, equip, marshal and house our army, navy and air force during the 1939-45 war. Certainly when you come to look at the amounts that we are spending now you would think the government of that period of 1939-45 had not provided any sort of armed forces and that Canada's defence effort had been almost completely negligible.
Now when we have armed forces of just about one-tenth of what we had in the peak of the war years, we are spending as though we had had practically no accommodation for the really enormous armed forces which we put into the field during those years. I think one is entitled to ask what has happened to all those buildings which were constructed during the last war. Some of the information we now get as to how they have been disposed of and as to the prices which have been received is really disturbing when you compare those figures with the cost of the present construction program.
From returns which were brought down this session I have taken four illustrations.
I know that buildings are subject to deterioration but I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these figures raise in our minds serious questions as to whether this money is being spent wisely or well. As to the four buildings here in Ottawa at the corner of Elgin and Argyle streets which were built at a total cost of $95,600, with fixtures worth $12,417 or a total of $108,017, those four buildings and all fixtures and equipment were sold for $10,000. There were two buildings at St. Hubert in Quebec which were built at a cost of $50,724.18 and sold a year or two ago for $5,600. There were three buildings at the same place built at a cost to the taxpayers of $99,386.35 and sold for $6,000.

Order. Are not these
figures the object of examination by the special committee on defence expenditures?
No, not these figures. None of these has been made the subject of inquiry by that committee; and so far as I know the agenda of the committee does not indicate that they are to be examined.
What have they to do with defence?

It is surprising to me that the minister will suggest they have nothing to do with defence, when he devoted such a relatively large part of his address this morning to a boastful revelation of the amount we were spending on defence construction, as a part of Canada's defence effort.
Then there were two other buildings in Montreal purchased as recently as 1948 for $29,000 and sold a year ago for $5,750. Those are examples of the way in which we have been disposing of buildings, which were built at heavy expense and sold for relatively small sums, and which would provide accommodation for our forces. In the case of the two buildings in Montreal we see that they were sold only three and a half years later for a fifth of the amount paid for them. Yet at the same time we are devoting hundreds of millions of dollars to constructing accommodation for the forces which have been raised as a result of the present program.
So I do not think the country can take much comfort from the fact that these huge sums are being spent on construction. Particularly is it true that the country cannot take comfort in the sense the minister would have the matter understood, namely that the construction of this accommodation is in some way or another a material contribution to the deterrent we are trying to build up against possible attack by the only potential aggressor that could attack Canada-that is, the Russians.
Then there are other features of the defence program, and the administration and handling of that program by the department, which give great concern to the people of Canada, and which it is our duty to bring up in the house with a view to obtaining an explanation. The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) referred only a few moments ago to the tendency toward empire building that seems to be going on in the defence department. He has given us some examples, and made particular reference to an increase in staff which appears to be entirely unjustified by the volume of work being done. I was particularly impressed by the increase in staff in the deputy
fMr. Fulton.]

minister's office. There may be some good explanation for these figures, but certainly I have not been able to think of it. I shall put the figures before the minister, and perhaps he will give us an explanation as to why these numbers should be on the staff now, as compared with the smaller numbers there during the war.
I have here a two-page return tabled in the house. It involves only one department, namely the Department of National Defence, and contains a question relating exclusively to the administration of the deputy minister's office here in Ottawa. This question stood on the order paper for quite some time, for at least a week or two, and finally, one day, it was answered. However, on the day it was answered it was made an order for return, as a result of which, of course, the answer did not appear in Hansard. I imagine that fact would probably give some comfort to the department, because the figures set out in the return are not particularly creditable to it.
This return was brought down on Monday, March 30, and it states that the total number at that time on the staff of the deputy minister of national defence was 114, whereas, during the war, as at March 31, 1944, the total number on the staff of the three deputy ministers for navy, army and air force was 98; as at March 31,-1945 it was 93 and as at March 31, 1946 it was 77.
To understand the significance of these figures we have only to mention the fact that in 1953 the department is administering a fighting force totalling 104,000, and for that task the staff of the deputy minister numbers 114; whereas in 1944 and 1945 they were administering fighting services totalling approximately 900,000, and for that purpose required staffs of only 98 and 93 respectively. In 1946, although demobilization had already commenced, there was still a substantial number of men in the forces over and above the number there now. In addition at that time they were faced with the extra problem [DOT] of demobilization. Yet in that year they were able to handle the work with a staff of 77 in the deputy minister's office.
In addition to that, there seems to be an unwarranted mushrooming of personnel, in comparison with the size of the armed forces, and particularly as compared with the numbers on strength during the war years. There now seems to be a tendency to resist giving full and complete information as to what is going on in the department, and what has been said about it by experts and others who have been appointed to examine into the affairs of the Department of National Defence.

We have seen examples in the house recently. We remember the refusal to give us copies of reports, and statements made with respect to those reports which have created a wrong impression. I would refer particularly to a report made by a member of the civil service commission on the activities in the establishment of the army works services, about which I attempted to get information on several occasions. Although it is known that a report does exist-and of course its existence is now established by authority of the statement by the Prime Minister-the house has not yet been taken into the confidence of the government; and thus far the government has refused to give us any other information as to what is in the report, or the circumstances under which it was compiled.
The other day I asked the Minister of National Defence if he would now table the full text of the report. His reluctance to give any information on the report, one which obviously is embarrassing to the government, is in strong contrast to some of his earlier statements as to the duties of governments and governmental bodies to give information, and as to the conclusions to be drawn when those bodies refuse to give information and let the people know the facts.
I had hoped the minister might show a great deal of frankness, and a readiness to co-operate with the house in this respect, in the light of a statement he is reported to have made at a meeting of the graduates of McGill University, and others held at South Porcupine, Ontario, on Saturday, March 6, 1948. I have here a mimeographed copy of the text, and the minister is on record as having said this at that time:
Communists cannot face facts. That is the reason why the communists will not allow us to go into their countries to see and report what is happening there, or tell their people the truth about what is happening here. They just cannot stand the comparison.
I regret very much that the minister who holds those views, views which are obviously correct, should not apply them in the case of his own department and welcome us into the department to see and report upon what is happening there. I hope it is not because he feels that the department could not stand comparison. It is unfortunate that statements were made in the house in connection with this particular report in reply to efforts we were making to get it, which certainly created a wrong impression. A statement was made by the Associate Minister of National Defence on March 4, as reported on page 2608 of Hansard:
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that if the hon. member is looking for an alleged report to which he
