Mr. Chairman, I do not propose at the moment to deal with the subject with which the hon. member for Kamloops was dealing just as he sat down, as apparently he intends to continue his remarks in connection with that matter and it can be dealt with fully when he has completed what he has to say.
I should like to deal briefly with another part of his speech this afternoon, the disposal of surplus buildings. As I understood the hon. gentleman, he was attempting to make some point that surplus temporary wartime construction was being disposed of at the present time under conditions that would indicate no justification for some or all of the present construction program being carried on to meet the present needs of the Department of National Defence.
The hon. member has placed a number of questions on the order paper in connection with the disposal of surplus buildings. It has been quite obvious from those questions that he has been interested in the disposal of wartime surplus buildings of a temporary nature, and that he has been interested particularly in the items in the annual report of Crown Assets Disposal Corporation which indicate that some buildings have been disposed of at fairly small amounts in comparison with the original cost.
The first point I should like to make is that the requirements of the Department of National Defence for construction at the present time obviously do not necessarily bear any relation to the requirements that the department faced under wartime conditions between 1939 and 1945. The requirements of our defence services have changed in the interim, and the whole program at the present time is a very different one. The construction program during the war was almost 100 per cent of a temporary nature, and I think nobody will deny that to make wartime construction of a temporary nature was obviously the proper and economical thing to do.
The second point is that at the present time there are certain requirements that can

be observed and recognized to be permanent. The fact is that prior to 1939 there was practically no permanent construction for the defence forces in Canada that had not been done by the British before they gave up their military responsibilities in this country. We therefore, in starting our defence program in 1950, were faced with very large requirements for permanent construction, and wartime temporary construction could not meet that need. Wartime temporary construction is continuing to be used wherever it can be used. It is being used in its present state in certain cases. In other cases, where circumstances require it, it is being made into a more permanent type of construction by means of the installation of foundations and things of that kind. In every instance where wartime accommodation can be used it is being employed, but in certain cases we are having to go into permanent construction for purposes of economy.
I think it is recognized throughout the construction industry and in every phase of Canadian life that when you have a longterm permanent requirement the cheapest and most satisfactory way to meet it is with a permanent, solid type of construction that does not carry with it the maintenance and ever-recurring costs that must be met with in less permanent types of constructions. So much for the suggestion in the hon. member's speech that for some strange reason we were not taking advantage of wartime temporary construction to the extent that we should.
Let us look for a moment at the question of the disposal of surplus buildings and what we get for them. It must be obvious to all hon. members that the value we get from construction is not to be judged by what the building will bring when its utility for the purpose for which it was intended has come to an end. The fact is that wartime construction served us extremely well and we got full value for the money spent on such construction from 1939 right up to 1946, 1947 and 1948 when our requirements for such buildings came to an end.
One example of the four given by the hon. member for Kamloops was the C.W.A.C. barracks at the corner of Elgin and Argyle streets, known as Argyle barracks. These barracks were built early in the war when the C.W.A.C. was first organized. They were used continuously while they were required for that branch of the army service and gave excellent value and good accommodation for the estimable young ladies who served in the C.W.A.C. in Ottawa during those years. When the C.W.A.C. was disbanded I understand the buildings were used for certain
Supply-National Defence temporary requirements, and then those requirements in turn came to an end. The problem was very simple. We either keep those buildings under crown ownership and let them stand empty and become a total loss or we try to sell them.
In a number of instances where there was a civilian use for wartime construction, the prices secured for the buildings were very reasonable and gave quite a nice return to the crown for the original investment. But in many cases, and the Argyle barracks was one of them, there was no civilian use. In fact they were put up for sale and there were no takers except those who were prepared to buy the buildings for the material they could salvage from them, in other words, those who were prepared to pay scrap value for the buildings. The means whereby we ensured that we got the best possible value out of these buildings was to put them up for sale by public tender. If the hon. member for Kamloops thinks that in the circumstances these buildings were worth more than the amount that was paid for them, and which he quoted from the annual report of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, he was perfectly entitled to go out and buy them and pay the price that he thought they were worth.
Himself.

Himself, or anybody else who might have wanted them. The fact is that those assets were put up for sale by public tender. We got the greatest amount of money for them that they would bring, and the result is that the crown has not only got out of the buildings the value of their service during the time they were occupied for army purposes, but they have also got the highest amount possible to get from them for scrap value. If the hon. member thinks there is any validity in any criticism that he has based on the questions he has placed on the order paper and the kind of argument he has made today, I submit he is very much mistaken.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with others who have already spoken in this debate in expressing the appreciation we all feel for the men and women of our armed forces who are performing a great service to Canada at home and abroad in these uncertain times. They constitute the shield behind which all of us can shelter. A review of the

Supply-National Defence world situation at the present time indicates that we cannot afford to relax our efforts in any way to build up our defences, and I am quite sure that all sides of the house, and for that matter the people of Canada generally, are in agreement on pushing forward the program for defence.
We are entitled, of course, to criticize the details of that program, but generally I think the feeling is one of desire that Canada play her full part in world affairs and protect not only her own territories and shores, but contribute to the defence of the free nations throughout the world.
The situation in Korea at the present time, although offering some slight prospect of relaxation of tension, is far from a solution. The exchange of sick and wounded prisoners is about to take place, but I noticed in the press of yesterday that rather extensive attacks by land, sea and air have been prosecuted by the United Nations forces, that the enemy's attacks on various portions of the front have been repulsed, and that strife is going on quite close to the place which those who are arranging the exchange of prisoners have selected. I notice, too, that even at this time with the prospect of some settlement held out before us, Canadians are back in action, and that Canadian casualties are again growing. It is not a prospect that leads one to hold out any hope for relaxation of effort.
This morning when the minister was making his statement I listened attentively, hoping that he would cover fully the situation in Korea. After all, we are making there our major effort in terms of danger to lives. I thought that his mention-it was not a review-of the Canadian situation was inadequate. I had hoped that he would give us a review of the last year's operations in Korea and draw our attention to the performance of our Canadian troops there, and generally point out, for the benefit of all of us and for Canada, the contribution that is being made by our forces under these difficult conditions. I had hoped that he would indicate the composition of our forces there in detail; that he would tell us the measures that are being taken to provide protection for our personnel in the field and comment on the standard of training and efficiency, and generally give us a picture of the war that is being waged in Korea.
I had hoped that he might say something about the use, if use is being made, of the Republic of Korea troops with our Canadian forces, as has been reported in the press. I had hoped that he would say something about the equipment of our men in the field and


the advantages, if any, of the type of protective clothing that has been developed for men serving in the line. I had expected that he would say something about the casualties suffered by our forces in Korea; but the mention of our casualties was confined to one brief sentence. As I recall the minister's remarks, he pointed out that 20,000 Canadians have participated in the engagements in Korea, and the rotation of units has taken place during the last two years. Then he said that of that number, 1,300 had been wounded. I think he intended to say that there had been 1,300 casualties.
I feel that more attention should have been paid to that particular aspect of the situation. As I say, it is our major effort from the standpoint of danger. Other efforts that we are making within Canada and abroad are vitally important; but nevertheless this does constitute the danger point of Canada's experience in warfare.
The casualty lists should be drawn to the attention of the House of Commons from time to time; we should not be dependent on the statements that appear in the newspapers. I notice that in today's paper the 171st casualty list was published, showing a total of 1,301 casualties under the headings of killed, 248; wounded, 939; missing, 26; injured, 87; prisoner, 1. That figure does not correspond with the return that was given to me and which appears in Hansard of February 9 of this year at page 1730, in response to my question. The answer that appears there says the total casualties to January 31 amounted to 1,335. I wonder why the difference, and whether there is not some explanation the department might give with regard to that. We should have accurate figures on the casualties occurring in Korea.
This is a heavy casualty list in 24 months of fighting. As I have pointed out before, the casualties have been suffered very largely by the 1,800 front-line troops of the infantry battalions, and a casualty list of 1,300 out of 1,800 men who appeared actively in the forward positions is heavy indeed.
From time to time I have been endeavouring to get information on another problem, namely that of ammunition. I notice that the minister's statement today with regard to ammunition was contained in one sentence. He was speaking about equipment and said something about the fact that we would meet our commitments with regard to guns, and then added that the same thing applies to ammunition. It would be advantageous, 1 think, if a complete report on the ammunition situation were available to the House of Commons.

On November 25 I asked a question of the minister concerning this matter, and on that occasion I was given a reply which is reported on page 63 of Hansard for that date. I should like to read two sentences from it, which are as follows:
But in this case our ammunition is supplied' from United States sources. We are on the United States supply line and get precisely the same treatment as the Americans get.
On December 5 the matter came up again, as the minister thought it necessary to rise at the opening of the house and make a statement in view of some remarks I had made earlier. On page 365 of Hansard for December 5, 1952, he had this to say with regard to ammunition:
So far as ammunition is concerned, the position in Korea is precisely as I outlined it the other day. Canadian troops have never been subjected to unnecessary casualties by any shortage of ammunition, nor are they in the least likely to be exposed in such a manner.
On March 9 I again returned to this problem because of the reports in the press throughout November, December, January and February concerning the shortage of ammunition in Korea. On that date I questioned the Associate Minister of National Defence, and his reply is reported on page 2736 of Hansard for that date. He said:
-there is no shortage of ammunition in respect of actual operations.
Then when I asked if the minister was aware of the declaration of General Van Fleet concerning the ammunition shortage in Korea, he replied again as follows:
I have no intention of commenting on any dispatches or any statements with reference to the ammunition supply of other nations.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if the Minister of National Defence informs the House of Commons that we are on the supply line of the United. States, then it is quite competent for members of the house to ask questions if that supply line seems to have failed in any respect, and we are entitled to answers with regard to that problem. It is not an answer to say that the problem of some other nation with regard to ammunition is not a matter for discussion in this house. If we are dependent upon the United States supply line for ammunition, then we are entitled to know what ammunition is being supplied to our forces, and that was the basis of my query.
Quite a bit of information concerning the ammunition shortage in Korea has come to light since the return of General Van Fleet from that theatre of operation. He was in command of the United Nations army there for two years, and under his command were the Canadians. In U.S. News and World Report for April 3 there is a lengthy verbatim 68108-244
Supply-National Defence report of the questions asked of General Van Fleet and the answers he gave concerning the situation in Korea and the alleged shortage of ammunition. General Van Fleet declared time and again during the course of that inquiry that there was a shortage of ammunition during the time he was in command in Korea, and that from time to time he had to issue orders restricting the use of ammunition. I am asking the minister to give to the House of Commons a complete report, some time during the discussion of his estimates, with regard to ammunition. Are our forces in Korea on the United States supply line for ammunition, or are they on a British supply line?
Information has reached me to the effect that a great portion of the ammunition supplied to our artillery in Korea has come from Canadian sources. Why can we not have that information, if that is correct? I have heard that during 1952 a very large quantity of ammunition was shipped from Canada to Korea. Why can we not have that information here? Let us have the facts. I am speaking of shells for the artillery. I notice that in General Van Fleet's discussion of the problem, mortar shells were often in short supply, as were grenades. The infantry soldier is dependent upon the supporting fire of mortars, and his use of grenades when he is in a difficult position under enemy attack. If the artillery is unable to supply the defensive fire which is required to repel an enemy attack, the infantry unit is dependent wholly upon its own supporting weapons, its mortars, its machine guns and the grenades in the hands of the individual soldier.
A little earlier I referred to the fact that the minister, in replying to me some time ago, had said that no Canadian troops had ever been subjected to unnecessary casualties due to a shortage of ammunition. It depends, of course, on how you view the situation. A somewhat similar question was asked of General Van Fleet by Senator Saltonstall, and the report is contained in U.S. News and World Report for April 3, at page 83. The questions and answers are as follows:
-were lives lost because we failed to send enough ammunition or was it that you just could not advance?
General Van Fleet replied:
The lack of ammunition means that you do not shoot as much as you wish, that you do not shoot at all the targets of opportunity; that when the enemy is firing at you, you do not fire a sufficient amount to silence his fire, counter-battery; that you do not maintain fire superiority on the battlefield because you cannot shoot enough that you would like to shoot, and all our regimental, all our battalion commanders, division, corps, and myself

Supply-National Defence would like to shoot more, and the more you shoot, the more enemy you kill, and the more American lives you save; that is just axiomatic.
I think any person who has served actively is well aware of that fact. If the artillery has an insufficient quantity of shells they cannot undertake counter-battery work, and counterbattery work is most effective in protecting your own troops from enemy fire. You may argue, and statements appear in the press, that there has been a sufficient quantity of ammunition in Korea for, as it is put in military terms, the mission given to the troops. But I say this. If the mission assigned to the troops is simply to sit in their trenches and take it because there is not sufficient ammunition to deter the enemy from firing their artillery at these troops, then that is not a very satisfactory mission on which to be engaged. It is far better to put in the hands of those troops the arms and ammunition that is required so they can dominate the field.
General Van Fleet reports that the enemy have doubled the number of guns on their front now as compared with the guns of the United Nations army. He reports that they may not have as much ammunition as has our side, nevertheless it is a fairly serious situation. He reports that it has resolved itself into an artillery war, and that greater emphasis is placed upon artillery than on any other branch of the service. It follows therefore that ammunition must be supplied for that type of conflict. He similarly treats of shortages that developed with regard to hand grenades and mortars. Just to indicate his awareness of the situation, at page 84 he says:
Because of that small supply or critical-below the critical level-by the end of December, I had practically prohibited anyone using 81-ram. ammunition except in extreme emergency.
That is evidence from the army commander that there was a shortage of some types of ammunition. In another place, at page 89, in answer to a question as to whether the method of operation at the front was dictated by the control of ammunition, General Van Fleet said:
It naturally influences everything we do along the front; the less ammunition you have, the less pressure you put on an enemy.
l am wondering what is the situation today with regard to our forces in Korea. They have just re-entered the line. A press dispatch from there says they have to regain control of no man's land and again gain domination of the battlefield area. Have they the arms and the ammunition with which to do that, or must they sacrifice lives? Must we have a lengthening casualty list because men have to go out and patrol under those conditions without adequate fire support? That is


the type of information we want and should have, I think, with regard to our forces which are serving actively in the field.
The problem of ammunition does not stop at that point. A press dispatch appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of March 18, 1953, coming from the Associated Press at Paris and referring to the meeting of the foreign ministers of the NATO nations who are to gather together on April 23, says this:
The critical shortage in all categories of ammunition will be the biggest headache facing the foreign ministers of the fourteen NATO nations when they gather in Paris April 23 for their second meeting in four months.
So perhaps we are facing an ammunition shortage in Europe as well as elsewhere. What is the ammunition situation right here in Canada?
The third matter with which I intend to deal, Mr. Chairman, is the balance of forces within the Canadian army. We have had put before us a great defence program for the defence of this country and for our commitments elsewhere. We have had painted for us a picture of developments in a great many fields of activities in the three services. I propose to deal now only with the Canadian army.
I think that in the last three years we have achieved within the Canadian army an unbalance of forces which is serious. In the Canadian army there are four main fighting groups, namely the infantry corps, the artillery, the engineers and the armoured corps assisted by the various services whose work is essential and is always conducted in an able manner. But the four fighting groups are those that I have mentioned.
What has happened owing to the policy that has been laid down by the minister? I am dealing now with high policy which rests right with the minister himself. As a result of the program, we have an infantry brigade in Korea and an infantry brigade in Europe. The second rotation now taking place in Korea provides that by this year three brigades of infantry will have gone through a baptism of fire under war conditions in Korea. The other brigade will have completed intensive training in Europe. All told, it means that four brigades of infantry will have received some form of intensive training or of actual active service.
In the artillery we have a regiment in Korea and a regiment in Europe. Rotation of the regiments, I presume, will result by this summer in four regiments of artillery receiving intensive or active service training and experience. I suppose a similar situation prevails with regard to the engineers, although their services may not have been called upon to a great extent; I am not aware of that.

Nevertheless they are, 1 presume, through rotation, getting a somewhat similar experience.
Let us consider the armoured corps, with one squadron in Korea and one squadron in Europe. By rotation not more than four squadrons have been exercised either in intensive training in Europe or under active service conditions in Korea.
What are the training results that come from a program of this nature? Let us consider the situation. Approximately four infantry brigades have been trained. Four brigadiers have received training. Twelve infantry commanders, lieutenant colonels, have received intensive training. Twelve majors, second in command of battalions, have been trained in an active theatre. Forty-eight majors, company commanders, have been trained actively. The infantry corps of the Canadian army must be at an extremely high state of trained efficiency, and I think that is all to the good.
But what about the armoured corps? It has become the Cinderella of the Canadian army. Not one lieutenant colonel has received training in an active theatre of war or intensively in Europe. He has no command. What training is there for a major in command of a squadron in Korea or in Europe? The white paper informs us that in Europe the infantry units are formed into three regimental combat battalions supported by tanks. It means that the tanks of the squadron there are farmed out to the infantry regiments. How does the major in command of that squadron ever exercise his squadron as a whole? I presume the same thing applies in Korea.
The importance of this matter becomes evident when you consider what is being brought about. Not only is it important that the junior officers, N.C.O.'s and men be thoroughly trained under active service conditions but it is even more important that the senior officers receive adequate training. That is being done in the infantry corps and, as time passes, from those trained senior officers in the infantry corps will be drawn the brigadiers and major generals of the Canadian army of the future. The artillery and the engineers may supply their quota of senior officers. But what opportunity is there in the armoured corps for advancement of any officer? There is no expansion of the armoured corps, and there is no opportunity for lieutenant colonels or brigadiers to be trained.
As time goes on we will find that the higher positions within the Canadian army are going to be filled by men who are unfamiliar with the armoured corps. I maintain that there 68108-244J
Supply-National Defence is a clear lack of balance in the training program of the Canadian army. What a difference there is between the situation now and the situation as it was at the time of the second great war. We had overseas three infantry divisions, two armoured divisions, two army tank brigades, three armoured reconnaissance regiments, two armoured car regiments and other armoured units. In summary, the Canadian army overseas was about half drawn from the infantry corps and half from the armoured corps. And that, I think, is a reasonable division of responsibility within a modern army.
At the present time the Canadian army is overweighted in infantry. The armoured corps is neglected. Compare the British army of today. They have eleven divisions undergoing training and performing services in various parts of the world. At least three of those divisions are armoured, and they are serving in Europe at the present time. They have maintained an armoured regiment with the commonwealth division in Korea, and have rotated. From the Royal Tank Regiment they have armoured units attached to the various infantry divisions, and they are maintaining a balance between their infantry forces and their armoured forces.
I suggest that the opportunity is now and for some considerable time has been in the hands of the minister. This is the plan I suggest to him, to maintain a proper balance: an infantry brigade in Canada; an infantry brigade in Korea; an armoured brigade in Canada and an armoured brigade in Europe. This would provide for the necessary rotation and replacements.
What could be done immediately? It would be reasonable to dispatch to Korea an armoured regiment. Send the Lord Strath-cona's Horse or the Royal Canadian Dragoons to the commonwealth division, and replace the British armoured regiment that is there. Or make plans for the dispatch to Europe of an armoured brigade to replace the infantry brigade now in that area. By that means a balance in our army would be maintained, and the training of our officers would be performed as it should be performed.
There is nothing more disturbing in warfare than to have a senior officer in charge of formations of which he has had little experience. Hon. members will recall that we went into the war of 1939-45 totally unprepared for armoured warfare. We had ignored the exploratory work that had been done by the British. We had ignored completely the efficient build-up of armour that had been conducted by the Germans; and we were caught totally unprepared. It was an extremely difficult matter for Canada to raise,

Supply-National Defence equip and train armoured formations. Fortunately we had several years in which to do it. We may not have that time available on another occasion, and I suggest that we should profit by the lessons of the past, and put our emphasis on these two major formations within the Canadian army, namely our trained infantry and our trained armour.
What is our final objective? Surely the lesson of the second great war is this, that if you are going to fight effectively you must have armoured formations. The white paper indicates that plans are afoot for the provision of a large training area in New Brunswick, where it will be possible to train formations of divisional strength. Are we to do that just on the basis of an infantry division? Surely not in this age. Armoured divisions, mobile forces, are what are required. And that is why I suggest we are missing a great opportunity at this time. It is unfortunate that we are involved in a war in Korea, and that heavy casualties have to be suffered there; but the opportunity is there to train men under active service conditions. It is unfortunate that we have to station men in Europe; but that provides an opportunity to give intensive and useful training to large formations.
Surely we must attempt to re-establish the balance in the Canadian army that we had during the second great war, and put proper emphasis upon the use of armour. In fact I have advocated in the house before this, and will continue to advocate in the future, that still greater emphasis should be placed upon a mobile armoured force. This has also been brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) and by others on more than one occasion. The mobility of an infantry division in conjunction with an armoured division can be greatly increased if that infantry component is provided with the proper type of armoured tracked vehicles to keep up with the armoured force. There is a great future for a mobile armoured force of that nature; and I think Canada most certainly should be in the forefront of progress along that line.
I shall not deal with other problems connected with the balance of forces within the Canadian army, but will be content to leave the matter there. I repeat that the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps has become the Cinderella of the Canadian army, and something should be done immediately to bring it back to the position it should occupy. We must produce officers in the Canadian army not only for infantry formations, but also officers trained in the use of armour as well as artillery. We cannot do that unless we


produce the means whereby they may gain that experience.
Time.
Go on.

We are spending billions of dollars in providing camp installations of all kinds. We are stockpiling soft goods, as they are called. We are doing something with regard to arms and ammunition, but we have not the full story even yet. I hope we will get it. And all of this will be ineffective unless the highest efficiency is obtained in our military formations and in their training.
Canada's shield of defence is to be found in her young men of military age. They deserve the best type of weapons and the best type of training. Of vital importance is the complete training of the senior officers; and that training is not being provided with the present lack of balance of forces within the Canadian army.

And if I did not give them that credit, it is obvious from their speeches that they are claiming credit for it themselves.
I happen to have in my riding the best army camp in the Dominion of Canada. I would include the
world in that as well. It is doubtful if anyone would include the city of Toronto in the world.

What I really wanted to say was that we have the finest airport in

Canada in the riding of Fraser Valley. We spent $5,491,887.86-we keep very close track of it-on that airport. I urge the Minister of National Defence to make use of this airport. I am not doing this in a spirit of warmongering, but simply because this third largest city in Canada is situated on the most vulnerable spot of the Pacific coast if we are ever attacked. Under these circumstances surely an airport such as that should be made use of.

Supply-National Defence privilege of showing him through the stainless steel kitchen. I do not want it to rust for lack of use. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I made the statement attributed to me by the hon. member for Kamloops and I meant exactly what I said. I was speaking for the department which I then represented, and I do not think it is in order for the hon. member to read a further meaning into my words beyond the ordinary meaning of the words which I used and which I meant.

The words the minister used are now on record in the course of this discussion. That, I point out, was on March 4, which would be five days after certain extracts from the report had been quoted in the press. These extracts, from which I shall quote shortly, raised very serious considerations as to the efficiency of the Department of National Defence. I doubt if either of the ministers would suggest, and certainly I would not suggest, that the government would be so completely indifferent to the implications or import of these passages that they would not be making fairly strenuous efforts to determine whether such a report was made, exactly where it was and the circumstances under which it was made. If it was discovered that there never had been such a report or memorandum or writing they would not have lost very much time in denying the existence of the report and in telling the house that there was no such writing in the possession of the government.
But not very long after that I had occasion to refer to this matter again in the house; that was on March 12. At that time I was challenged to produce the report, to which I replied that the government had the report and that I had asked them to produce it, and if they denied the accuracy of anything I was saying then I suggested they produce the records and prove that what I said was inaccurate. That challenge, I might say, was not taken up by the government.
Four days later, on March 16, these extracts which had appeared in the press, and the existence of the report, were again referred to. On that occasion the Prime Minister intervened and said, with reference to the earlier statement by the Associate Minister of National Defence, that the hon. gentleman had stated that there was no report of which these excerpts, referring to the excerpts that had appeared in the press, would be extracts. On the same date he also said there had been no indication of where these excerpts had come from.
This was on March 16, some 18 days after the appearance of these quotations in the press. I suggest to you sir that if the Prime Minister was able to state that there was no

report of which these excerpts would be excerpts, and was able to reinforce what the Associate Minister of National Defence had earlier said, that there were no such reports in the possession of the Department of National Defence, it is then very obvious that the government had been making pretty intensive inquiries to ascertain what were the true facts. As every hon. member will agree, and as I will be the first to maintain, when the Prime Minister makes a statement on a matter which is within his knowledge as prime minister and head of the nation, then that statement must be accepted and we accept the fact that it is a statement made on his responsibility as Prime Minister.
I doubt very much if it would be proper- certainly it would not be accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite-for us to suggest that the Prime Minister would make that statement without having been informed that pretty intensive inquiries had been made within the department and by the government as a whole. I think I should interject here that the report in question was a report made by an official of the civil service commission concerning establishments as the result of a request made by the Department of National Defence, and a report made as the result of a survey of the army works service and the establishment of that service, which was the object of the request by the Department of National Defence. The report was made and it was in the possession and under the control of the government, as the Prime Minister's subsequent statement revealed.
But it is important to realize that at three o'clock in the afternoon of March 16 the Prime Minister made a statement which threw very grave doubts upon the accuracy of an earlier statement that had been made from this side of the house concerning the report; and he made that statement some 18 days after the matter had first become a subject of controversy in the house and a subject of discussion in the press. I raise very seriously the question of whether the government knew anything more about that report at 3.30 on the afternoon of March 16 than they knew about it at 3 o'clock on the afternoon of March 16. Are we to suppose that after 18 days of intensive search and inquiry as to the existence of the report, as to its whereabouts and the circumstances under which it was made, the government was in complete ignorance at 3 o'clock and yet at 3.30 that same afternoon knew all about it? I suggest to you, sir, that that supposition does not stand up; but if that is the case, then I would expect and would
Supply-National Defence welcome verification from the government that those were the circumstances.

As I was saying, Mr. Chairman, the report made by the official of the civil service commission who made a survey-

no, not that. I hope you will not accept that.

shows circumstances found and reported upon to be exactly as those that were found by Mr. Currie. We have this particular extract:
I came to the conclusion that number six works company must be known in Halifax by workmen as a good place to get a soft job and a good place for third-class tradesmen to roost to their heart's content.
I am not doing this with any desire to make an invidious distinction as between one locality or another. I took these two excerpts because they do prove conclusively that the situation at Halifax was known to officials in the employ of this government two and a half years before Mr. Currie made his investigation. When Mr. Currie made his investigation, he found exactly the same circumstances at Halifax as well as at other places. It is particularly because the incidents at Halifax proved the truth of that general assertion that I have referred to them.
I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question?

Up to the moment I have been making these remarks under considerable difficulty. I wonder if the hon. member would reserve his question until a later stage, or until I have concluded this part of my remarks?

I shall be delighted.

What Mr. Currie said is reported at page 728 of Hansard for December 15, 1952. It reads as follows:
As an example of what can be and actually has been done to remedy conditions quickly, it is interesting to follow the action which was taken at Halifax immediately following my inspection early in September. I reported verbally to national defence headquarters that conditions at Halifax were not satisfactory. As had been found at other establishments, stores, accounting and administrative procedures had broken down seriously. Senior officers were immediately dispatched from Ottawa to look into the situation. They took remedial action at once. Certain key personnel were replaced; others were put on notice; temporary stores and clerical staff together with a labour force were engaged to clean up the situation and bring the accounting records up to date.
In November, I was invited to return to Halifax to examine the results of the vigorous action which had been taken. I found that remarkable changes had been made. The company had been completely reorganized.
A little later on he said:
As a result of what had been done the unit had been placed in a position to function properly and to carry on with normal efficiency.
So, Mr. Chairman, what happened was this. In April, 1952, Mr. Currie was appointed to investigate the whole situation in the army works services. He found a chaotic condition at Halifax, exactly the same as that reported in September, 1949, by Mr. MacNab. Mr. Currie outlines the situation here. He tells the officials in the department what the circumstances are, and by now the matter has reached such proportions the department knows it cannot keep this under the cover any longer, so active steps are taken to deal with the situation at Halifax. Only three months later Mr. Currie says that he goes back to Halifax and finds that effective action has been taken.
Now, when we apply that situation to the whole of the Currie report, in which he reports on the administrative breakdown in the Department of National Defence and in which he says that at various army works service establishments he finds this chaotic condition, you can see, Mr. Chairman, how important this is, and how unfortunate it is that the government did not take effective action in September, 1949 to deal with the situation which was then drawn to its attention but which it preferred to ignore. Effective action was taken as a result of Mr. Currie's inquiry because the matter had come into the realm of public knowledge and public discussion, and could not be kept under the carpet any longer. A report was in their possession as long ago as September, 1949, yet they did nothing about it.
Of course, various attempts are made to minimize this matter and say that this is not


a report at all but merely a memorandum. When the matter becomes one of public knowledge and public discussion, officials of the department write to reporters objecting to what those reporters may say about it.
In this connection I think the public should be, and is, very much concerned. Certainly my impression is that the public is very much concerned about the way in which the Minister of National Defence has sheltered behind his deputy, and has allowed and encouraged his deputy minister to make representations which should have been made by the minister. Let there be no doubt about the situation in this regard. To criticize what has happened in this case is not to criticize the civil service. It is to criticize the government for not cleaning up affairs in its own department initially, and then leaving things in a position where civil servants feel that they have to enter the lists of controversy in order to defend things that are going on in their department.
Just two days ago we were told by the Minister of National Defence that he approved the writing of the letter by the deputy minister, and that places upon the minister the onus of a very serious charge. It is the charge of using the civil service in a manner in which it is most improper for the government to use it. If the deputy minister felt keenly about this and wanted to write such a letter, that is a matter which can be understood. But if the minister approved that course of action, and in fact encouraged it, I submit to you that would be a most improper course of action for a responsible minister of the crown to take. If there were things which required to be said regarding this matter of public political controversy, it was for the minister to say them and not his deputy.
I am glad to note that the deputy did go to the minister before he wrote the letter. As I have said, his motives and his feelings with respect to what was going on are matters we can appreciate, because he is a normal person. But the fact that the minister would allow him to fall into what I suggest was an error and would, in fact, encourage him to do so, thus leaving the responsibility on his deputy instead of assuming it himself, is most reprehensible.
In this connection I do not leave it, sir, on the basis that I am a constitutional expert. I base my position on a book which is accepted as the authority on the British constitution, written by Mr. Ivor Jennings, in which at pages 143 and 144 you find the following passages:
The responsibility of ministers to the House of Commons is no fiction, though it is not so simple

as it sounds. All decisions of any consequence are taken by ministers, either as such or as members of the cabinet. All decisions taken by civil servants are taken on behalf of ministers and under their control. If the minister chooses, as in the large departments inevitably he must, to leave decisions to civil servants, then he must take the political consequences of any defect of administration, any injustice to an individual, or any policy disapproved by the House of Commons. He cannot defend himself by blaming the civil servant. If the civil servant could be criticized, he would require the means of defending himself. If the minister could blame the civil servant, then the civil servant would require the power to blame the minister. In other words, the civil servant would become a politician. The fundamental principle of our system of administration is, however, that the civil service should be impartial and, as far as may be possible, anonymous.
I am quite sure, Mr. Chairman, there is not a member of the house on either side who, if he but reflects upon the matter, would not agree with that statement of principle. Yet the minister has made two if not more most important departures from that principle, and has taken actions which place him in direct violation of the principle of independence of the civil service. He has encouraged his deputy minister to take action with respect to a matter which is in the realm of political controversy, which is going to involve the department and the civil service in criticism. Jennings says that if the civil servant can be criticized, he would require the means to defend himself.
It is one of the principles of our government that civil servants do not speak on matters of policy. They do not have the means of defending themselves. It is therefore important-and I make this statement with due regard for its implications-that in the House of Commons we should avoid criticizing civil servants with respect to matters of government policy. Our criticism should be directed toward the government. When the minister encourages his deputy minister, his senior civil servant, to take a position with respect to a matter of political controversy, then he inevitably and most improperly exposes that civil servant to criticism in the house. I am not going to say anything beyond that point. My quarrel is with the minister and with the government, not with the civil servant who was led into placing himself in that position.
Then Jennings goes on to say:
If the minister could blame the civil servant, then the civil servant would require the power to blame the minister.
There is controversy here. There are criticisms in connection with the letter which the deputy minister wrote to Mr. Stevenson because of the facts which I have put on the records of the house regarding the circumstances surrounding this MacNab report. Yet the minister encouraged the writing of that
Supply-National Defence letter. The minister has told us that he approved the letter and said, "Yes; go on and write it". I think it is most extraordinary that the minister did not say, "I will sign that letter; the responsibility is mine, not yours". The minister is now in a position to say, and has to say, that any fault or inaccuracy or otherwise is, of course, in the deputy minister's letter. He says it is perfectly accurate. There is a controversy as to that.
What controversy?

What position is the minister left in? He has to say, "That is a letter of my deputy". It is a letter of his deputy. So if there is any blame to be attached or any criticism to be made, the situation would be that the minister would have to blame the civil servant. But it is not open to a civil servant to answer, or to blame the minister. So we have a complete breach and a complete disregard of two of the most important principles with regard to the position of the civil service. The fact is that as a result of this course of action what is likely to happen is just what Jennings has said:
hi other words, the civil servant would become a politician. The fundamental principle of our system of administration is, however, that the civil service should be impartial and, as far as may be possible, anonymous.
Is that the Jennings of the restaurant?
I did not hear what the hon. member said. What did he say?
Something silly.
I am not sure whether or not the remark will appear in Hansard,', but as I did not hear it, I cannot answer it.
I asked whether that was the Jennings of the restaurant.

If the hon. member for
Fraser Valley thinks that Mr. Jennings of the restaurant-estimable character though he may be-is an authority on constitutional matters, I shall leave him to continue in that belief. However, I do not think he holds it seriously and I greatly doubt that any other member of the House of Commons would not know the Jennings to whom I was referring.
The situation is this. Since this matter first came up, that is to say, the question of the Currie report itself and the question later on of the MacNab report and all these various matters involving criticism of his department-the Minister of National Defence has been, I submit, too prone to leave responsibility with those who should not be required to bear the political responsibility, and he
3856	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence still owes to the house a great many things by way of explanation with regard to the circumstances surrounding this whole matter. He owes us an explanation as to why they chose to disregard the MacNab report. He owes us an explanation as to why they chose to leave the impression with the house and the country that there was no such report; and why it was that they did not do anything to remove that impression until after the evening edition of the Ottawa Journal of March 16 proved beyond a doubt that there was such a report and that the government could no longer get away with the fiction it was trying to maintain in this matter, and indeed in connection with the whole matter of national defence.
The minister and his associate owe a duty not only to the house but to the country to take it into their confidence and to stop trying to indicate to the people that they are getting value for their money when we find that, far from that being the fact, an unnecessarily large proportion of what is being spent for defence is being spent on frills and fancy things which are not going to deter any potential aggressor from his desire to attack, if that should be his desire. And they owe an explanation as to why it is that the government-which now, in spite of its own efforts, has had a few comers of the rug lifted so that a few glimpses of what is underneath the rug have been vouchsafed to the people of Canada-should still persist in trying to sweep more things under the rug and then to hammer more tacks into the edge of the rug so as to keep the people in ignorance of the true state of affairs with respect to national defence.	.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to delay the committee for many minutes because everything the hon. member for Kamloops has said has already been answered in Hansard. I refer to the statement of the Prime Minister on March 16 which appears at page 2968 of Hansard, and also to the other statements that have been made. To that I have little to add at this time, beyond this. The hon. member has raised the matter of this so-called MacNab report two or three times, I think, in another place, and two or three times in this chamber. It is rather important that it should be understood just what this report was. I suggest that the best source of that information is what Mr. MacNab himself said about it as reported in the London Free Press of March 17, 1953.
Who was interviewing him?
Oh, you were not interrupted.
Not more than a dozen times.

The article is headed "Private Letter Lawyer States" and reads as follows:
Ronald S. MacNab, former staff investigator for the civil service commission and now a London lawyer, denied last night that a memorandum he wrote in 1949 was a government report. He said it was'a private letter to his superior, and statements in it were not necessarily facts, but-
And the reporter quotes this:

"things I had heard from various sources during the course of routine investigation.''
Mr. MacNab was reported in Ottawa yesterday as the author of one of the controversial "reports" which opposition members have sought as alleging waste and extravagance in the defence department.
Contacted in London, Mr. MacNab said he wrote a private letter to George T. Jackson, director of organization and classification for the civil service commission, in September, 1949, on the request of Mr. Jackson. In it, Mr. MacNab said, there were statements-not charges nor facts as such-which he had heard from army and other sources.
"But it was not a government report," he emphasized. "Before it could be a government report these statements would have had to be checked and double-checked."
This is the document which somehow, by means unknown, was extracted from the files of George T. Jackson of the civil service commission or was given by someone unknown into the hands of the hon. member for Kamloops or Mr. Arthur Blakely, the correspondent of the Montreal Gazette, and which then was produced not at the committee on defence expenditure when it might have been produced-
It was refused there. It was asked for and was refused by the government majority.
It was asked for, but by a person who probably had a copy of that memorandum in his own possession, whereas the Department of National Defence had never had a copy in its possession.
Or the rest of the government?

The rest of the government, either. This was a personal document prepared for Mr. George T. Jackson who, as the Prime Minister said in his statement on March 16, happened to be in Burma, and consequently it was some time before any trace was found of the source of this story as it appeared in the Montreal Gazette, from some source unknown to the government, quoting sections of this statement. On the basis of that the hon. member for Kamloops has on two occasions taken up the time of this house and held up the defence expenditure committee to talk about reports and concealment and so on.
I suggest to him that the business of this country demands that we give most serious

attention to the affairs of national defence; that we look into every charge for which there is any basis, and that we investigate it to the full, as we have. People talk about receiving hundreds of letters. How many letters have been brought to my attention during the last six years relating to irregularities? How many? You could count them on the fingers of one or two hands. Every one of them has been investigated; and in every case where an investigation has shown that there has been wrongdoing, the prosecutor has been the government and the Department of National Defence. We have taken that course in every case where it appeared to be justified.
Now we have these continued sweeping assertions without support and without corroboration.- In this instance a report dating from 1949, four years ago, is now paraded before us as something that the government is endeavouring to conceal, when the government did not even know of its existence.
The Prime Minister knew about it on March 16.
Because at about that time Mr. Jackson's secretary looked in his private file.
Then the government should know of its existence.

I am prepared to answer other questions that were put by hon. members in the course of the serious discussion this afternoon. I would be happy to do so, unless there are other hon. members who wish to speak. I must say that the course of the debate this evening has indicated that there is an intention rather not to allow me to make this reply tonight.
Sir, the business of the defence of our country is serious business. As hon. members have said, we have defence forces fighting in the field today, and I suggest that that business is serious; and that hon. members before attacking the effectiveness of our operations either abroad or at home by making assertions for which they are unwilling to take personal responsibility, should think twice about its effect upon our national effort.

If the minister wishes to have an answer, I take the responsibility, as I have said before, for the assertions I have made. And I will give the minister an answer now, if he wants to have one, or later, if he wishes.
Produce the letter.

The minister seeks to brush this whole incident aside as something based not upon any memorandum or report, but merely a private letter. As I have said
Supply-National Defence before, when is a report not a report? Perhaps it is when it is embarrassing to the government.
The minister has read from a Canadian Press dispatch of a reported interview with Mr. Jackson in London. I asked him the source of that dispatch, and he did not indicate what it was. I happen to have read it, and I know it is a Canadian Press dispatch giving, in abbreviated form, the gist of a reported interview. But there is in existence and on the record a very much fuller report of an interview with Mr. MacNab. This was an interview by Mr. Richard Jackson of the Ottawa Journal, containing the observations made by Mr. MacNab in reply to his questions. This particular portion is not in quotation marks, but it is what Mr. MacNab said. The newspaper article states-
He left the government service In 1949, but not before verbally reporting to Mr. Jackson-
That is Mr. George Jackson.
-conditions he had found in army camps.
At Mr. Jackson's request, he committed his findings to writing in an official memorandum after he had left the civil service staff but was still in Ottawa.
Since that time-
The actual time of that incident is not reported in this article.
*-tire memorandum has been shown to deputy defence minister C. M. Drury.
That is not correct.

It continues:
Tracing Mr. MacNab's moves since he left Ottawa in 1950, the Journal this morning found him by long distance telephone at his London law office.
Were you the author of the disputed MacNab report? he was asked.
"Why, is it now causing a stir?" he countered. "Yes, something of a stir in parliament.
"Some people say it was an official report, others claim it was a personal letter; which was it?" asked the Journal.
"It was neither. It was a memorandum." "Written before or after you left Ottawa?" "Written after I had left the civil service commission, but while I still was in Ottawa."
"Why did you write it after you had left the government staff?"
"I was instructed to."
"By whom?"
"By Mr. George Jackson. I had reported verbally to him on the findings of my investigations and he ordered me to put them in a memorandum."
"Did it just cover conditions you found in army establishments at Halifax?"
"No, it covered a number of other centres.''
"Do you regard it as an official report made in line of duty as a civil service investigator?"
"Yes. I suppose I must. But why don't you ask Mr. Jackson about it?"
Then there is an interjection by Mr. Richard Jackson who wrote the article, where he states:
Mr. Jackson is on a special government assignment in Burma, advising the Burmese government in civil service problems.
3858	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence The interview continues:
"Is there any doubt that your memorandum reported a condition of waste and extravagance in army encampments?"
"You'd better read the report yourself".
Then the article continues:
The memorandum was written (at Mr. Jackson's request) as a matter of "routine", further explained Mr. MacNab.
Every two years, civil service staff investigators probed the use each department made of staff.
Then the article continues with observations by Mr. Richard Jackson on other subjects of controversy. So it is pretty certain that this was not a private letter. It was a memorandum reducing to writing personal observations made by Mr. MacNab when he was touring army works services establishments in the course of his official duties. If the minister wants to perpetuate this fiction that it was not a report based on personal observations, but was merely hearsay, I suggest to him that to do so is merely to insult the intelligence of the house. All you have to do is to read what was said in that memorandum as quoted in the press. The accuracy of what was quoted has not been questioned in any way. Of course they cannot question its accuracy.
Does the hon. member take responsibility for the accuracy of that quotation?

I have told the hon. member on two occasions previously, and I now say to him for the third time, that I take responsibility for the accuracy of everything I have said. If the hon. gentleman disputes its accuracy let him go to the government and require the government to table the text of the report. Until he does that I wish he would cease these futile and childish interruptions and show some sense of responsibility in connection with this matter. Here is what the memorandum says:
The slowness of the tradesmen (at Halifax) is a standing joke in the garrison. As an example I was shown a plywood partition about six feet wide and told that it actually took four carpenters two weeks to build it.
Here is another one:
While I was interviewing in the area engineer's office in Regina (one whole day) the entire staff was idle, many were sitting at their desks, soldiers and civilians, no work of any sort on the desks.
I ask the hon. member and the minister if that is hearsay. I ask them further how they reconcile-

speechtext:
Order. Perhaps I should point out that when the hon. member for Kamloops says, "I am asking the hon. member", when he puts a question he should at the same time indicate when he wants the hon. member for Halifax to answer. Otherwise 

it becomes provocative and perhaps the hon. member for Halifax is justified in trying to take the floor in order to answer.
There will be another question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Kamloops has the floor but if in the course of his remarks he says, "I ask the hon. member for Halifax," perhaps the hon. member for Halifax should wait until the hon. member for Kamloops, who has the floor, indicates when he wants him to answer.

I welcome the hon. member's question, but I was in the course of putting another one to him and I thought he might like to answer them both at the same time. I should like to hear also from the minister. After all, it is the Minister of National Defence to whom we are putting these questions. If the hon. member for Halifax wishes to assume responsibility for that department as well, he is welcome to do it. My other question is this: Will the minister, the associate minister and the hon. member for Halifax explain how they reconcile the fact that what Mr. MacNab said in his memorandum was on all fours with what Mr. Currie subsequently reported. Are they going to say that Mr. Currie's report is based on hearsay?
Mr. Currie did not say anything about that. You can search his report and you will not find anything to that effect.

So far as the question submitted to me is concerned, I might say that the very point covered by the minister was what I intended to raise a few minutes ago when the hon. member would not agree to my asking a question. It is quite obvious from the quotations he gave from this personal letter of Mr. MacNab's and from the Currie report that there cannot be the slightest connection between the two incidents.
In answer to his question about hearsay I would simply point out that anybody who has the slightest knowledge of what hearsay is and what direct evidence is, on reading the quotations which the hon. member put on the record from the MacNab letter, will say that what he says there is based upon what he was told had happened some time previously. If that is not hearsay, then I do not know what it is.
You do not.

Apparently the hon. gentleman does not know what is hearsay; and if he wants to indulge in self-accusation, that is all right by me. It will be remembered that Mr. Currie said that the appalling conditions at Halifax were the same sort of conditions

that had been reported upon in the MacNab report. Mr. Currie said:
I reported verbally to national defence headquarters that conditions at Halifax were not satisfactory. As had been found at other establishments, stores, accounting and administrative procedures had broken down seriously.
Those things are in amplification of and are exactly similar in nature to the very incidents mentioned by Mr. MacNab.
Oh, no.
Mr. MacNab is even more specific than Mr. Currie. He reported on particular incidents which he noticed at Halifax.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What somebody told him.

He said, "I saw". He said that at Regina when he was interviewing, the whole staff was idle, that many soldiers and civilians were sitting with no work on their desks. That was a personal observation. He further said this:
The engineers (R.C.E.) are engaged in some very large (construction) projects and I think it is fair to say that their attitude toward costs of construction indicates their attitude to finance generally, including money spent on staff. It seems to me that they are under the impression that . . . cost is no object when they want to do something.
That is in language exactly similar to the report of Mr. Currie, who states, as reported on page 717 of Hansard:
This involves the abandonment, by all administrators of the program, of the war psychology with its emphasis on speed with resultant wastefulness and extravagance-
The findings of the two men throughout their reports proceed on parallel lines. If the government wishes to draw the absurd distinction that in one case it was not a report because it was a memorandum, whereas in the other case it was a report because it was entitled a report, they can rely upon that sort of distinction; but it shows that they are driven to that sort of absurdity to justify their position.
The facts placed on the record and the facts found by Mr. MacNab and reported by him, as well as his own conclusions based upon his personal observations, establish clearly that these matters were found and were reported, not to a minor or obscure official but in the first instance to the director of organization of the civil service commission. Is anyone going to say that he is a minor or obscure official? I should not think the government would say that.
Then as to the minister's statement that the answer to all this is found in the statement made by the Prime Minister on March 16, to be found at page 2968 of Hansard; that is no answer at all. Indeed it proves,
Supply-National Defence if anything more were needed, that the government did know about this report; that it sought to leave the impression that there was no such report; that it knew about it at 3 o'clock on March 16 yet still refused to set out the full facts; that it left the impression with the house that there was not such a report or if there was one, which they doubted, they did not know anything about it.
The statement made by the Prime Minister at 3.30 showed that they had known just as much at 3 o'clock as they knew at 3.30. But they revealed their knowledge at 3.30 only because their hands were forced by the article which appeared in the afternoon edition of the Journal of that day.
What the minister has said is no answer to the serious criticism we are making. There may be room for controversy as to whether or not the mere incidence of the MacNab report reporting on conditions in the army works services would be sufficient justification for a sweeping condemnation of the whole defence department; but when you find that what is said in the MacNab report is substantiated and confirmed by what is said in the Currie report; when you find that the government is so anxious to suppress the facts regarding the MacNab report, indeed its very existence; when you find that they will say at 3 o'clock on March 16 words which leave the impression that there is no such report and then have to eat those words at 3.30, I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that the basis of our condemnation and criticism of the department has been amply established.
No answers?

Mr. Chairman, in the few minutes remaining I should like to get back to matters other than that which has been discussed for the last hour. I want to refer to some of the items that were dealt with in a general way by the minister earlier today. I listened to his statement with a great deal of interest, and it was encouraging to note that when given even half a chance Canadian youth are able to put forth a fairly substantial effort in the defence of freedom and the values that make up our way of life. The record established in world war I was maintained in world war II, and it is evident that the pioneer spirit is by no means dead in this country.
As I listened to the rather general statement of the minister I felt the same sense of frustration that I have experienced on other occasions when defence matters have been discussed in the house. I do not think I am as frustrated as the hon. member for Kamloops because he has a real problem and he
3860	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence has been here longer and has had a greater opportunity to become frustrated. However, I have discovered in my short experience in the house that it is rather difficult to dig out information from the Department of National Defence dealing with what might be described as problem areas. I have found that in most cases it is necessary to go to magazine or newspaper reports in order to get any information that might be regarded as helpful. I felt that such was again the case this afternoon as I listened to the general statement of the minister.
The phrase "not in the public interest" seems to be resorted to very frequently by the government, and perhaps the Department of National Defence abuses the privilege more than any other department. I am sometimes led to believe that instead of saying "not in the public interest" it should say "not in the government's interest" or "not in the party's interest". I had that experience of frustration at the beginning of March when I was trying to seek out information with respect to welfare services in the armed forces. At that time a resolution that I had placed on the order paper for the production of papers was denied. Access to that information was denied me as a private member. Previous to that, on November 27 last, I asked a question on the orders of the day with regard to the same problem. My question was as follows:
In view of the continuing expansion of the armed forces, does the government intend to make use of the welfare facilities offered by the voluntary organizations which served so effectively during world war II?
In reply the minister said:
The heads of the three services consider that it would be unwise, uneconomical and unnecessary to establish at all these places-
The reference is to the various Canadian military establishments.
-the five welfare agencies that we used during the second world war and I agree with them.
I suppose that is where the matter would have rested if we on the opposition side had been inclined to accept the statement as

definitive. But I find that the matter is not at all settled. It would seem that even the Department of National Defence itself is not completely happy over the present situation, because in the answer to a question I placed on the order paper on February 25 there was some indication that resort is being had to welfare facilities other than those found within the military organization itself. Part 3 of my question was as follows:
What facilities are provided for entertainment, recreation and welfare for these personnel and who provides these services?
The reference is to our air force personnel stationed in France. The answer to question No. 3 reads in part as follows:
To assist in recreational planning, the R.C.A.F. has on loan from the government of Ontario an expert in adult education and recreation. He is now in France to organize recreational and entertainment programs.
That would indicate that the trend toward militarization of welfare, if I may use that phrase, has not been entirely satisfactory in its results. Again, I notice that the Canadian Legion makes use of a phrase that was used in reference to my question of November 27 and quotes it in an article found on page 17 of the Legionary. The heading is, "Unwise, Uneconomical, Unnecessary". The Legionary quotes excerpts from a letter written by the Minister of National Defence in reply to an inquiry with respect to whether the department intended to use the auxiliary services of the Legion.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
